as if carved, as if ground."
2.6 The *Zhuan* says:
What is the reason for rain after praying for rain (yú)?
It is said:
There is no reason.
It is like rain falling even without praying.
When a star falls and trees moan,
the people of the country are all afraid.
Why?
These are changes of Heaven and Earth,
transformations of Yin and Yang,
things that rarely occur.
It is permissible to be surprised by them,
but not to fear them.
Solar and lunar eclipses,
the appearance of strange constellations,
untimely winds and rains,
these are things that no age has ever been without.
If the ruler is wise and the government is just,
even if these all occur together, there will be no harm.
If the ruler is foolish and the government is dangerous,
even if none of these occur, there will be no benefit.
Of all the calamities that befall all things,
the calamities caused by people are the most to be feared.
What are the calamities caused by people?
Plowing poorly harms the crops;
weeding poorly harms the harvest;
If the government is dangerous and loses the people,
if the fields are overgrown and the crops are poor,
if the price of grain is high and the people are hungry,
if there are dead people on the roads,
if bandits and thieves rise up together,
if those above and those below are estranged,
if neighbors assault each other,
if people steal from those across the street,
if ritual and righteousness are not cultivated,
if cattle and horses interbreed,
if the six domestic animals produce monstrous offspring,
if ministers and subordinates kill their superiors,
if fathers and sons suspect each other—
this is called human anomaly.
This arises from disorder.
The *Zhuan* says:
"The disasters of Heaven and Earth
are those hidden and neglected,
the anomalies of all things
are not recorded in books.
Transformations that are useless,
calamities that are not urgent,
discard them and do not govern them."
As for the righteousness between ruler and minister,
the affection between father and son,
the distinctions between men and women,
they are to be diligently refined and never abandoned.
The *Shī* says:
"As if cut, as if polished;
as if chiseled, as if ground."
2.7 Kǒngzǐ said:
"The mouth desires savory flavors,
the heart desires ease,
teach them with benevolence (rén).
The heart desires peace,
the body dislikes labor,
teach them with respect (gōng).
If one loves argument and is fearful,
teach them with courage (yǒng).
The eyes love beauty,
the ears love sound,
teach them with righteousness (yì)."
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"Keeping the back still,
separating the spine, danger inflames the heart."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Alas, young lady,
do not indulge with men."
All of these prevent evil and prohibit indulgence,
harmonizing the mind and will.
2.8 A high wall, broad at the top and narrow at the bottom,
will not necessarily collapse.
But when descending rain rises up
and flowing floods arrive,
then collapse will surely come first.
If the roots and shoots of grasses and trees are shallow,
they may not necessarily be uprooted.
But when a whirlwind arises,
and a torrential rain falls,
then uprooting is sure to happen first.
If a ruler resides in a state,
but does not value rén (仁, benevolence) and yì (義, righteousness),
respect virtuous ministers,
and govern the myriad things with reason,
it may not necessarily perish.
But once an extraordinary change occurs,
and the feudal lords engage in conflict,
people rush and chariots race,
and disaster arrives imminently,
only then do they begin to worry,
with parched throats and scorched lips,
looking up to the sky and sighing,
hoping perhaps to achieve security—
isn't it too late?
Kǒngzǐ (孔子, Confucius) said:
"Not being cautious beforehand and regretting it afterward—
alas!
Even if you regret it, it's too late."
The *Shī* (詩, Book of Poetry) says:
"To gather up one's tears—
what lamenting is of any use?"
2.9 Zēngzǐ (曾子) said:
"The junzi (君子, gentleman) has three sayings
can be strung together and worn.
The first is being distant to those within and intimate to those outside;
the second is blaming others when one's own conduct is not good;
the third is crying out to Heaven only after disaster has arrived.”
Zǐ Gòng said,
“What does this mean?”
Zēng Zǐ said,
“To be distant to those within and intimate to those outside,
is this not a reversal?
To blame others when one’s own conduct is not good,
is this not a great departure?
To cry out to Heaven only after disaster has arrived,
is this not too late?”
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says,
“Bitterly they weep,
How can lamenting avail?”
2.10 Now, frost, snow, rain, and dew
are what kill and give life to all things,
but Heaven does nothing in this,
yet we still value Heaven.
Enforcing laws and disliking elaborate writing,
governing officials and governing the people
are the affairs of officers;
the ruler does nothing in this,
yet we still respect the ruler.
Now, opening up land and planting grain was Hòu Jì’s task,
and controlling the flow of the Jiāng and Hé rivers was Yǔ’s task,
and hearing lawsuits and holding to the middle ground was Gāo Yáo’s task.
However, one who has a sage's reputation is Yáo 也.
Therefore, if one governs with the Dao,
even if one is personally incapable,
one will certainly make capable people work for oneself.
If one governs without the Dao,
even if one is very capable,
it will still be of no benefit to survival or demise.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"Holding the reins as if they were ribbons,
the two outside horses dance."
It values the ability to govern.
2.11 The *Zhuàn* (Commentary) says:
Confucius 孔子 said:
"How admirable is the charioteering of Yán Wúfù 顏無父!
The horses know that there is a carriage behind them, so they move lightly; they know there is a person above them, so they love him.
The horses are intimate with his correctness and love their work.
If horses could speak,
they would surely say:
'How joyful
is today's groom!'"
As for Yán Lún 顏淪,
he is slightly diminished.
The horses know that there is a carriage behind them, so they move lightly;
they know there is a person above them, so they respect him.
The horses are intimate with his correctness and respect their work.
If horses could speak,
He will certainly say:
"The groom is coming,
he is the one who makes me work!"
As for Yán Yí 顏夷, he has declined.
A horse knows there is a carriage behind and bears its weight,
knows there is a person above and fears him.
The horse is close to its handler and fears its job.
If a horse could speak,
it would certainly say:
"Groom, come!
Groom, come!
If you don't groom,
he will kill you."
Therefore, there is a method to controlling horses,
and a way to governing the people.
If the method is obtained, then the horses are harmonious and happy;
if the way is obtained, then the people are peaceful and gather together.
The *Shī* 詩 [Book of Odes] says:
"Holding the reins like silk cords,
the two trace horses move like dancing."
This is what it means.
2.12 Yán Yuān 顏淵 was attending Duke Dìng of Lǔ 魯定公 on a terrace,
and Dōngyě Bì 東野畢 was driving horses below the terrace.
Duke Dìng 定公 said:
"Excellent!
Dōngyě Bì's 東野畢 horsemanship is excellent!"
Yán Yuān 顏淵 said:
"It is good, it is good.
However, those horses will soon run away."
Dìng Gōng was displeased
and said to his attendants,
"I have heard that a gentleman does not slander others.
Could it be that a gentleman also slanders people?"
Yán Yuān withdrew.
Shortly after, the stableman reported that Dōngyě Bì's horses had run away.
Dìng Gōng threw aside his mat and stood up,
saying,
"Quickly prepare a carriage and summon Yán Yuān."
Yán Yuān arrived.
Dìng Gōng said,
"Earlier, I said,
'How excellent is Dōngyě Bì's horsemanship!'
You said,
'It is good, it is good,
but those horses will soon run away.'
I don't know how you knew this?"
Yán Yuān said,
"I knew it from the way he governs.
In the past, Shùn was skilled at employing people,
and Zàofù was skilled at employing horses.
Shùn did not exhaust his people,
and Zàofù did not overwork his horses.
Therefore, Shùn had no people who fled,
and Zàofù had no horses that ran away.
Now, when Dōngyě Bì
Ascending the carriage and grasping the reins,
the posture and bearing are proper.
Turning and maneuvering, pacing to and fro,
the courtly rituals are complete.
Passing through dangers and reaching afar,
the horse's strength is exhausted.
Yet, one still urges it on without ceasing;
that is how one fails to understand its distress."
Dìng Gōng said:
"Good,
can you elaborate a little?"
Yán Yuān said:
"When a beast is cornered, it bites;
when a bird is cornered, it pecks;
when a person is cornered, they deceive.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been a case where one has exhausted the lower ranks without facing danger.
The *Shī* says:
'Holding the reins like cords,
the two outer horses are like dancing.'
This speaks of skillful driving."
Dìng Gōng said:
"It is my fault!"
2.13 Cuī Zhù assassinated Duke Zhuāng,
and assembled the officials and grandees to make an alliance.
Those who made the alliance all removed their swords before entering.
If one's words were not swift,
and the blood was not applied immediately,
He died,
after killing more than ten people.
Next, it came to Yàn Zǐ.
Holding up a cup of blood,
he looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"Alas!
Cuī Zhǔ is about to commit a lawless act and murder his lord."
Thereupon, all those who had sworn the oath looked at him.
Cuī Zhǔ said to Yàn Zǐ:
"If you join me,
I will share the state with you.
If you do not join me,
I will kill you.
Straight spears will push you,
and curved spears will hook you;
I hope you will consider this."
Yàn Zǐ said:
"To remain for personal gain and betray one's lord is not benevolent;
to be coerced by blades and lose one's will is not courageous.
The *Shī* says:
'The spreading creeper,
extends to the branches.
The kind and gentle lord,
seeks fortune without turning back.'
How could I turn back?
Straight spears push me,
He bent his weapon to hook him,
but Yīng did not change his mind about it."
Cuī Zhǔ said:
"Release Yàn Zǐ."
Yàn Zǐ rose and went out,
was handed the mounting rope and got into the carriage.
His servant drove swiftly.
Yàn Zǐ stroked his hand and said:
"The elk and deer are in the mountains and forests,
but their fate lies in the kitchen.
Fate is determined;
why rush so quickly?"
Walk calmly to fulfil the moral principle,
and then leave."
The *Book of Odes* says:
"The lambskin coat is as if soaked (with sincerity),
Truly upright and virtuous.
That son of ours,
Gives up his life, not stealing (from his duty)."
That is about Yàn Zǐ.
2.14 King Zhāo of Chǔ had a retainer named Shí Shē,
as for his character,
he was impartial and loved straightforwardness.
The King made him a judge.
Thereupon, on the road there was a murderer,
Shí Shē pursued him,
and it was his father.
Returning to the court, he said:
"The one who committed murder
was my father.
To establish governance based on my father
is not filial piety.
To not carry out the ruler's law
is not loyalty.
To relax punishment and abolish the law,
and then evade its consequences,
is what your servant must uphold."
Thereupon, he submitted to the axe and block,
saying:
"My life is in the hands of my lord."
The lord said:
"Pursuing him but not catching him,
how could there be guilt?
You, just manage affairs."
Shí Shē 石奢 said:
"Not so.
Not being impartial to one's father
is not filial piety.
To not carry out the ruler's law
is not loyalty.
To be spared from a death sentence
is not integrity.
That my lord wishes to pardon him
is a favor from above.
That I cannot disregard the law
is righteousness from below."
Thereupon, he did not avoid the axe and chopping block,
and slit his own throat and died in the courtyard.
Gentlemen, hearing of this, said,
"How righteous is this man of law,
this Shí Xiānshēng!"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The son conceals for the father,
the father conceals for the son,
uprightness is found within this."
The *Shī* says,
"That son of others,
is the chief justice of the state."
It speaks of Shí Xiānshēng.
2.15 Outwardly lenient but inwardly upright,
placing oneself within the compass and square,
being upright towards oneself but not upright towards others,
being good at withdrawing and not feeling resentful—
this is the conduct of Qū Bóyù.
Therefore, those who are fathers wish to have him as a son,
those who are sons wish to have him as a father,
those who are rulers wish to have him as a minister,
those who are ministers wish to have him as a ruler,
his name shining among the feudal lords,
the world desires him.
The *Shī* says,
"That son of others,
is a worthy man of the state."
This is the conduct of a *jūnzǐ*.
2.16 The *Zhuàn* says:
Kǒngzǐ encountered Chéng Běnzi of Qí between Yǎn,
stopped his carriage and spoke with him for a whole day.
After a while,
he turned to Zǐlù and said:
"Yóu!
Present the gentleman with ten bolts of silk."
Zǐlù did not respond.
After a while, he turned again and said:
"Present the gentleman with ten bolts of silk."
Zǐlù abruptly replied,
"In the past, I, Yóu, heard from you, Master,
that gentlemen do not meet without proper reason,
nor do women marry without a matchmaker;
such conduct is not proper for a *jūnzǐ*."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Does the *Shī* not say:
'In the fields are spreading grasses,
the dew is heavy.
There is a beautiful person,
with clear brow and gentle grace.
We met by chance,
fulfilling my desire.'
Moreover, Chéng Běnzi of Qí
is a worthy gentleman of the world.
If I do not present him with a gift,
zhōng shēn bù zhī jiàn yě.
Dà dé bù yú xián,
xiǎo dé chūrù kě yě."
2.17 A jūnzi has a heart for excelling at goodness,
but does not show an air of surpassing others.
His virtue is sufficient to govern the world,
yet he has no arrogant or unrestrained appearance.
His actions are sufficient to reach future generations,
yet he does not criticize the faults of others with a single word.
Therefore it is said:
The jūnzi is full of virtue yet humble,
emptying himself to receive others,
acting widely without being swayed,
responding to things without being exhausted.
Even when in a low position,
the people are willing to support him.
Even if he wishes not to be respected,
is that possible?
The *Shī* says:
"That son of his,
beautiful as an Ying flower,
beautiful as an Ying flower,
so different in his public conduct."
2.18 A jūnzi is easy to get along with but
difficult to become familiar with,
easily awed
but cannot be coerced,
fears trouble
Not avoiding righteous death,
loving profit
but not doing what is considered wrong,
associating with relatives
but not forming cliques,
speaking eloquently
but not being confused,
how magnanimous! It's easy not to lose him,
how firm! He is upright but not cutting,
how warm! The light of his benevolence and generosity is great,
how surpassing! He has something that distinguishes him from the world.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Beautiful as jade,
beautiful as jade,
remarkably different from the nobles."
2.19 Shāng Róng once held a feather flute
and relied on infantry,
wanting to attack Zhòu but being unable.
So he left
and hid in the Tài Háng Mountains.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn
and established himself as the Son of Heaven,
he wanted to make him one of the Three Dukes.
Shāng Róng declined, saying:
"I once relied on infantry,
wanting to attack Zhòu but being unable.
I am foolish.
Not contending and hiding,
He had no courage.
Foolish and without courage,
(I am) not worthy to fill the position of one of the Three Dukes."
Thereupon, he firmly declined and did not accept the appointment.
A gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"Shāng Róng may be said to have
examined himself inwardly and not exaggerated his abilities.
A true gentleman!
He is far from being a freeloader.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
'That gentleman there,
Does not eat idly.'
It speaks of Master Shāng."
2.20 Marquess Wén of Jìn sent Lǐ Lí to be the Grand Justice.
Erroneously judging a case, (he) caused a man to be killed.
He confined himself in the courtyard,
requesting death from the ruler.
The ruler said:
"Offices have high and low ranks,
Punishments have light and heavy degrees.
If a subordinate official is guilty,
It is not your crime."
Lǐ Lí replied:
"I occupy the position of chief official,
I do not yield my position to subordinate officials;
I receive a great deal of emolument,
I do not share the profits with subordinate officials.
"To carelessly listen and cause someone to be killed,
and for a subordinate official to bear the responsibility for his death,
is something I have never heard of."
He did not accept the order.
The ruler said:
"If you consider yourself guilty,
then I too am guilty."
Lǐ Lí said:
"If the law is not upheld, then punishments are flawed,
and if punishments are flawed, then people die.
Your Majesty considered me capable of discerning subtle points and resolving doubts,
therefore you appointed me to administer justice.
Now, having carelessly listened and caused someone to be killed,
the crime I have committed deserves death."
The ruler said:
"To abandon your position and relinquish your office,
to submit to the law and cause the state to perish,
is not what I desire.
Leave quickly!
Do not trouble my heart."
Lǐ Lí replied:
"A disordered government and a perilous state
are the worries of the ruler.
A defeated army and a chaotic soldiery
are the worries of the general.
Now, being unable to serve the ruler well,
and blindly holding office,
It is to eat the salary without merit.
Your subject cannot falsely accuse himself with emptiness."
Thereupon, he lay on his sword and died.
A gentleman, hearing of this, said:
How loyal!
The *Shī* says:
"That gentleman,
Does not eat white rice."
This refers to Mr. Lǐ Xiānshēng.
2.21 The madman of Chǔ, Jiē Yú, tilled the land and ate from it.
His wife had gone to the market and not yet returned.
The King of Chǔ sent an emissary
to bring one hundred *yì* of gold to his door,
saying:
"The Great King has sent your subject to present one hundred *yì* of gold,
wishing to invite you, sir, to govern Hénán."
Jiē Yú laughed but did not respond.
The emissary, therefore, could not speak his farewells and departed.
His wife came from the market,
and said:
"Sir, you were righteous when young,
how can you abandon it when old?
How deep are the chariot tracks outside the door!"
Jiē Yú said:
"Today, the king sent an emissary to bring one hundred *yì* of gold,
wanting me to govern Hénán."
His wife said:
"How could I allow it?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
His wife said:
"If you disobey the ruler's orders,
it is not loyalty.
If you obey them,
it is abandoning righteousness.
It would be better to leave."
Thereupon, the husband carried a cooking pot and stove on his back,
the wife carried scriptures on her head,
they changed their surname and given name,
and no one knew where they went.
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
"When the color changes, they fly up,
circling before they settle."
This is the wife of Jiē Yú.
The *Shī* says:
"I will leave you,
and go to that land of joy.
Land of joy, land of joy,
where I will find my place."
2.22 In the past, Jié made a pool of wine and a levee of distiller's grains,
indulged in extravagant music,
and had three thousand people drink like oxen.
All the ministers held each other and sang, saying:
"The Jiāng River is overflowing!
The boats and oars are broken!
"My king is ruined!
Hurry back to Bó!
Bó is also great!"
He also said:
"Happy, happy!
The four steeds are proud!
The six reins are glossy!
Leaving what is not good to follow what is good, good—
why is it not happy!"
Yī Yǐn knew that the great mandate was about to depart,
raised his cup and approached Jié, saying:
"If the ruler does not listen to the words of his ministers,
the great mandate will depart!
Ruin is just around the corner!"
Jié clapped his hands in agreement
and burst out laughing,
saying:
"You are speaking like a sorcerer again!
I possess the empire,
just as Heaven possesses the sun.
Can the sun perish?
If the sun perishes, I will also perish."
Thereupon, Yī Yǐn, putting on his shoes, hastened away,
and then went to Tāng.
Tāng made him his minister.
It can be said that he went to that happy land,
and there he found his place.
The *Shī* says:
"Soon I will leave you,
and go to that land of joy.
Land of joy, land of joy,
there shall I find my place."
2.23 Yī Yǐn left the Xià and entered the Yīn.
Tián Ráo left Lǔ and went to Yān.
Jiè Zǐtuī left Jìn and went into the mountains.
Tián Ráo served Duke Āi of Lǔ
but was not recognized.
Tián Ráo said to Duke Āi:
"Your subject will leave you,
the yellow swan is taking flight."
Duke Āi said:
"What do you mean?"
He said:
"Has Your Lordship not seen the rooster?
The one who wears a crown on his head is refined,
the one who spars with spurs on his feet is martial,
the one who dares to fight when an enemy is before him is brave,
the one who announces when he finds food is benevolent,
the one who keeps watch at night and doesn't miss the time is trustworthy.
The rooster has these five virtues,
yet Your Lordship still boils and eats him every day.
Why is this?
It is because its origins are near.
Now, the yellow swan, with one flight, travels a thousand *lǐ*,
stops in Your Lordship's garden pond,
eats Your Lordship's fish and turtles,
"They peck at your millet and sorghum,
but lack these five qualities.
Yet you still value them,
because their origin is distant.
Your minister is about to leave you,
the yellow swan is taking flight!"
Āi Gōng 哀公 said:
"Stop!
I will record your words."
Tián Ráo 田饒 said:
"Your minister has heard that one who eats its food
does not destroy its container.
One who seeks shade under a tree
does not break its branches.
If you do not use your minister,
what is the point of recording his words?"
Thereupon he left for Yān 燕.
Yān 燕 appointed him as its prime minister.
After three years,
the government of Yān 燕 was greatly at peace,
and the state had no thieves or robbers.
Āi Gōng 哀公 sighed deeply
and vacated his chamber for three months,
reducing his upper garments.
He said:
"To be careless in the beginning and regretful afterward,
how can one recover what is lost?"
The *Shī* 詩 (Book of Poetry) says:
"I shall leave you soon,
going to that land of joy.
Land of joy, land of joy,
where I can obtain my worth."
2.24 Zǐ Jiàn 子賤 governed Dānfù 單父 by
playing the bright zither,
not even stepping down from his hall,
and Dānfù 單父 was well governed.
Wūmǎ Qī 巫馬期 left with the stars
and returned with the stars,
not resting day or night,
personally attending to everything,
and Dānfù 單父 was also well governed.
Wūmǎ Qī 巫馬期 asked Zǐ Jiàn 子賤.
Zǐ Jiàn 子賤 said:
"What I do is called entrusting people,
what you do is called entrusting strength.
Entrusting people is easy,
entrusting strength is laborious."
People say Zǐ Jiàn 子賤 is truly a gentleman,
relaxing his limbs,
preserving his ears and eyes,
calming his mind and breath,
and all the officials are well-managed,
simply entrusting them to their responsibilities.
Wūmǎ Qī 巫馬期 is not like that.
Sighing, [he attends to] affairs personally,
exerting effort to instruct and admonish.
Even though he governs, he still has not reached the highest level.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"You have clothes and robes,
Do not drag them, do not be careless with them.
You have carriages and horses,
Do not race them, do not drive them recklessly."
2.25 Zǐ Lù said:
"If a *shì* (gentleman) cannot endure hardship,
cannot take death lightly,
cannot be content with poverty,
and yet says, 'I can practice righteousness,'
I do not believe him."
In the past, Shēn Bāo Xū stood in the court of Qín,
for seven days and seven nights,
his crying did not cease,
and thus he preserved Chǔ.
If one cannot endure hardship,
how can one achieve this?
Bǐ Gān was about to die,
yet his remonstrations became even more loyal.
Bó Yí and Shū Qí starved on Shǒuyáng Mountain,
yet their resolve became even more evident.
If one does not take death lightly,
how can one achieve this?
Zēngzǐ wore coarse hemp clothing with tattered ends,
never having a complete garment.
He ate coarse rice,
never being full.
If righteousness is not in accordance,
then resign from the position of senior minister.
If one cannot be content with poverty and destitution,
how can one practice this?
Now, if a scholar wishes to establish himself and practice the Way,
he must not consider difficulties,
and then he will be able to practice it.
If one wishes to practice righteousness and make a name for himself,
he must not consider profit or harm,
and then he will be able to practice it.
The *Shī* says:
"That son of those people,
is great and sincere."
If not a gentleman who sincerely cultivates himself and practices it,
who can compare to him?
2.26 Zǐlù and Wūmǎ Qī were gathering firewood at the foot of Yùnqū.
A wealthy man from Chén, named Chǔ Shīshì,
had a hundred carriages with greased axles
at a banquet on top of Yùnqū.
Zǐlù said to Wūmǎ Qī:
"If you were not to forget what you know,
nor further your abilities,
and obtain this wealth,
never again seeing the Master for the rest of your life,
would you do it?"
Wūmǎ Qī sighed, looked up to the sky, and exclaimed,
and threw his sickle to the ground with a *tà* sound,
saying:
"I once heard it from the Master:
'A brave warrior does not forget losing his head;
A man of determination and benevolence
does not forget being in a ditch.'
Do you not know me?
Are you testing me?
Or is it their will?"
Zǐ Lù 子路 felt ashamed,
so he carried his firewood home first.
Confucius said:
"Yóu 由!
Why did you come back before everyone else when you went out together?"
Zǐ Lù 子路 said:
"Earlier, Yóu 由 and Wūmǎ Qī 巫馬期 agreed to gather firewood
below Yùn Qiū 韞丘.
There was a wealthy man from the Chù 楚 state named Chù Shī 處師,
with a hundred carriages adorned with grease,
feasting on top of Yùn Qiū 韞丘.
Yóu 由 said to Wūmǎ Qī 巫馬期:
'If you were to not forget what you know,
nor advance what you are capable of,
and obtain this wealth,
and never see the Master again for the rest of your life,
would you do it?'
Wūmǎ Qī 巫馬期 sighed, looked up to the sky, and
heavily threw his sickle to the ground,
and said:
'I once heard the Master say,
A brave warrior does not forget losing his head;
a person of lofty ideals and benevolence
does not forget ending up in a ditch.
Do you not understand me?
Are you testing me?
Is it perhaps his ambition?"
Yóu also felt ashamed,
so he first carried firewood home."
Kǒngzǐ picked up the zither and played it.
The *Shī* says:
"The bustards flap their wings,
gathering on the thick oaks.
The king's affairs are never-ending,
and I cannot plant millet.
What do my parents have to rely on?
O distant blue Heaven,
where can I find solace!"
Is it that my Way cannot be practiced?
It makes you wish for it.
2.27 Kǒngzǐ said:
"A shì has five types.
Some have power and noble status,
some have wealthy families,
some have courageous and fierce resources,
some have wisdom and intelligence,
and some have beautiful appearances.
Those who have power and noble status,
If one does not
practice righteousness through loving the people,
but instead resorts to violence and arrogance;
if those with wealthy families
do not relieve the poor and rescue those in need,
but instead indulge in extravagance without restraint;
if those endowed with courage and valor
do not defend their superiors and engage in battle,
but instead use their strength to encroach upon others and engage in private feuds;
if those with intelligence and wisdom
do not use them for honest calculations and planning,
but instead engage in cunning and deceptive practices;
if those with beautiful appearances
do not use them to govern the court and oversee the people,
but instead use them to seduce women and indulge in desires;
these five are
what are called scholars who have lost their fine qualities."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Mild and warm as jade,
Yet dwelling in his rough house,
He throws my heart into disorder."
2.28 What those in positions of authority encounter,
they prioritize appearance,
then sound,
and lastly actions.
Therefore, that which causes one to appear fit to be a ruler is countenance;
that which makes one believable when near is appearance;
that which is reliable when spoken is words;
What endures and remains impressive over time is conduct.
Therefore, a ruler's countenance and bearing
become the model and image for the world to look to.
Without uttering a word, people know him to be the ruler.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"His face is like vermilion lacquer."
Is that not describing his ruler?
2.29 Zǐ Xià finished reading the *Shī*.
Confucius asked,
"What is it that you find so significant in the *Shī*?"
Zǐ Xià replied,
"The *Shī*, in its relation to affairs,
is as clear and bright as the light of the sun and moon,
as distinctly arrayed as the ordered procession of the stars.
It contains the Dao of Yáo and Shùn above,
and below, the righteousness of the Three Kings.
This disciple dares
not forget it.
Even living in a humble dwelling,
playing the zither and chanting the odes of the former kings,
whether there are people who enjoy it or not,
I still enjoy it.
It allows me to be so inspired that I forget to eat.
The *Shī* says:
'Beneath the gate of thorns,
one can linger and abide.
The Mì River flows vast and wide,
allowing one to find joy even in hunger.'"
The Master suddenly changed his expression and said:
"Ah!
You, my student, can now begin to discuss the *Book of Poetry*.
However, you have seen its exterior,
but have not seen its interior."
Yán Yuān said:
"The exterior has already been seen,
what more is there to the interior?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Peeking at its gate,
but not entering within,
how can you know where its hidden depths lie?
But understanding its hidden depths is not difficult.
I, Qiū, once devoted my heart and mind,
and already entered within it.
In front, there are high cliffs,
behind, there are deep valleys,
clear and distinct like this,
and then it is established."
Not being able to see its interior,
one cannot be considered to understand its essence.
2.30 The *Commentary* says:
If a state lacks the Way, then whirlwinds will be fierce and swift,
torrential rains will break trees,
the Yin and Yang energies will be disordered,
summer will be cold and winter warm,
spring will be hot and autumn flourishing,
The sun and moon lack light,
the stars and planets move out of order,
the people suffer from many illnesses,
the country experiences many misfortunes,
creatures do not live long,
and the five grains do not ripen.
During the time of Chéng Zhōu,
the *yīn* and *yáng* were balanced,
the cold and heat were moderate,
creatures thrived,
and all things were peaceful.
Therefore, it is said:
their customs were orderly,
their music was continuous,
their driving of horses was leisurely,
their people were content,
their pace was slow,
and their intentions were good.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"It is not the wind that causes it,
it is not the carriage that is jolting,
but looking back at the roads of Zhōu,
my heart is full of sorrow."
2.31 As for the methods of regulating *qì* and nourishing the heart,
if the blood and *qì* are vigorous and strong, then
strive for harmony and balance;
if wisdom and planning are deeply hidden,
then unify them with easy understanding;
If (someone is) courageous, resolute, strong, and decisive,
then assist them with principles and skills;
if (someone is) efficient, resourceful, and quick,
then settle them with tranquility and withdrawal;
if (someone is) humble, submissive, greedy, and seeking profit,
then elevate them with lofty aspirations;
if (someone is) tolerant of the masses and fond of dissipation,
then constrain them with teachers and friends;
if (someone is) lazy, neglectful, and prone to abandoning things,
then comfort them with (warnings of) misfortune and disaster;
if (someone is) sincere, gentle, upright, and honest,
then harmonize them with ritual and music.
In general, among the methods for governing one's *qì* and nurturing the mind,
none is more direct than through ritual,
none is better than acquiring a teacher,
and none is more wondrous than focusing on one thing.
If one focuses on one thing, then (one becomes) concentrated;
if (one is) concentrated, then (one becomes) refined;
if (one is) refined, then (one becomes) spiritual;
if (one is) spiritual, then (one) transforms.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* strives to bind the heart to one thing.
The *Shī* says:
"The virtuous person, the *jūnzǐ*,
their demeanor is focused.
Their demeanor is focused,
their heart is like a knot."
2.32 Jade that is not carved
does not become a useful object.
If people do not study,
they cannot become accomplished.
If a family has a thousand gold pieces worth of jade,
but does not know how to manage it,
it is the same as being poor.
If a skilled craftsman carves it,
then wealth will extend to sons and grandsons.
If a *jūnzǐ* plans for it,
then it will be used for the country.
Therefore, movement brings peace to the common people,
and deliberation extends the people’s lives.
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"The virtuous and good *jūnzǐ*,
is the standard for the people of the country.
Is the standard for the people of the country,
how could he not live ten thousand years!"
2.33 In the house of a family marrying off a daughter,
the candles are not extinguished for three nights,
because they are thinking of the separation.
In the house of a family taking a wife,
music is not played for three days,
because they are thinking of continuing the family line.
Therefore, wedding ceremonies are not congratulated,
it is the proper order for people.
After three months, she is presented at the ancestral temple,
to be called the "new wife."
The next morning, she meets her father-in-law and mother-in-law.
The father-in-law and mother-in-law descend to the western steps,
The woman ascends from the eastern steps to
be entrusted to the chamber.
Grieving and thinking for three days,
not eating meat for three months,
this is the feeling of a filial son.
Therefore, ritual is
a regulated pattern crafted in response to human emotion.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"The relatives tie her wedding sash,
ninety are her ceremonies."
It speaks of many ceremonies.
2.34 Investigate the decree of Heaven,
govern the techniques of the mind,
regulate likes and dislikes,
accommodate temperament and nature,
and the way of governing is completed.
Investigate the decree of Heaven,
and then one will not be deluded by misfortune and fortune;
not being deluded by misfortune and fortune,
then one's actions and stillness are ordered.
Govern the techniques of the mind,
and then one will not be recklessly joyful or angry;
not being recklessly joyful or angry,
then rewards and punishments will not be biased.
Regulate likes and dislikes,
and then one will not be greedy for useless things;
not being greedy for useless things,
Then it does not harm the nature of things.
To accord with one's feelings and nature
is not to overindulge in desires;
not overindulging in desires
is to nourish one's nature and know contentment.
These four things are not sought externally,
not borrowed from others;
they are turned inward to oneself and preserved.
The true human being is one who delights people,
whose form is manifested in rén 仁 (benevolence) and yì 義 (righteousness),
and whose actions become a model.
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
"When felling an axe handle, when felling an axe handle,
the pattern is not far off."
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* 韓詩外傳 (Han's Commentary on the Book of Songs) Chapter 3
3.1 *The Commentary* says:
In the past, when Shùn 舜 had no grease in his earthenware pots,
those below did not incur blame by having surpluses.
He ate from earthen bowls
and drank from earthen cups,
and the farmers did not incur blame by exerting their strength.
He wore deerskin clothing with a hemp collar,
and the women did not incur blame by being skillful.
When the laws are easy to follow,
and affairs are few, it is easy to achieve success,
and the people do not incur blame from the government.
Therefore, the Great Dao accommodates much,
Great virtue is often found in those who are lower in status,
and sages accomplish much with little action.
Therefore, their use of things is always effective.
The *Zhuan* (Commentary) says:
"By being simple
the principles of the world can be grasped."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"If governance is conducted with ease,
descendants will preserve it."
Loyalty makes ritual easy,
sincerity makes language easy,
worthiness makes governing the people easy,
and skillful craftsmanship makes using materials easy.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"If governance is conducted with ease,
descendants will preserve it."
3.2 In the time of the Yīn dynasty,
grain grew in the courtyard of Tāng,
and in three days it became as large as an armful.
Tāng asked Yī Yǐn,
"What is this thing?"
He replied,
"It is a grain tree."
Tāng asked,
"Why does it grow here?"
Yī Yǐn said,
"Grain that grows in the marshes is a wild thing.
Now it grows in the courtyard of the Son of Heaven,
It is probably inauspicious."
Tāng said,
"What should be done?"
Yī Yǐn said,
"Your servant has heard that omens are precursors to disaster,
and auspicious signs are precursors to blessings.
If one sees an omen and does good,
then disaster will not arrive.
If one sees an auspicious sign and does not do good,
then blessings will not come."
Thereupon, Tāng purified himself with fasting and resided in quietude,
rising early and sleeping late,
mourning the dead and inquiring after the sick,
pardoning faults and aiding the poor.
After seven days, the grain revived.
The evil omens disappeared,
and the state prospered.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Revere the might of Heaven,
and thereby preserve your position."
3.3 In the past, during the time of King Wén of Zhōu,
in the eighth year of his reign,
in the sixth month of summer,
King Wén fell ill in his chamber.
After five days, the earth shook,
in the east, west, north, and south,
not extending beyond the suburbs of the state.
The officials all said,
I, your subject, have heard that earth tremors
are related to the ruler of the people.
Now, our King is seriously ill,
and after five days, the earth trembled,
in all directions, yet not beyond the outskirts of the capital.
All the ministers are fearful
and request that we move it (the capital).
King Wén Wáng said:
"How could we move it?"
The reply was:
"Undertake construction and mobilize the masses to expand the city walls;
perhaps that could move it."
King Wén Wáng said:
"That is not acceptable.
For the way of Heaven is that the appearance of ominous signs
is to punish those who are guilty.
I must have committed some fault,
and therefore Heaven punishes me with this.
Now, to engage in construction and mobilize the masses
to expand the city walls
would be to increase my guilt.
This cannot lead to prosperity.
I request that we change our behavior, emphasize good deeds, and move it that way;
perhaps that way we can be spared."
Thereupon, he was diligent in his ceremonies and offerings of dressed hides and leather,
to make alliances with the feudal lords;
he refined his words and diplomatic messages,
and gifts of silk and fabrics,
To treat the outstanding scholars with propriety;
to bestow their ranks,
grades, and fields,
in order to reward those with merit.
Then, together with his ministers, he carried this out. After doing this for only a short time,
the illness stopped.
King Wén ascended the throne and in the eighth year, there was an earthquake.
Forty-three years after the earthquake,
he governed the state for a total of fifty-one years before his death.
This is why King Wén encountered the calamity.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Awe the majesty of Heaven,
and thus you will preserve yourself."
3.4 A king's discussion of virtue is
to not honor those without merit,
not appoint those without virtue,
not punish those without guilt,
the court has no positions by favor,
the people have no lives by luck.
Therefore, to value the wise and employ the capable
and grades are not overstepped,
to curb violence and restrain the fierce
and punishments are not excessive,
the people clearly all know
that doing good at home will earn rewards at court,
doing evil in secret will incur punishments in public.
This is called a settled principle.
This is a king's discussion of virtue. The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Míng zhāo yǒu Zhōu,
shì xù zài wèi."
3.5 The *Commentary* says:
To consider following custom as goodness,
to consider wealth and possessions as treasure,
to consider nourishing one's nature as one's own path,
this is the virtue of the common people,
not yet reaching the level of the *shì* (士, scholar-officials).
To implement the law with a firm resolve,
not allowing private desires to harm what one has heard (i.e., learned),
this is a strong *shì*,
not yet reaching the level of the *jūnzǐ* (君子, gentleman).
To implement the law with a firm resolve,
to love cultivating what one has heard in order to correct one's emotions,
speech and actions mostly appropriate,
but not yet peaceful and understanding;
knowledge and deliberation mostly appropriate,
but not yet comprehensive and thorough;
when in a superior
position, one can amplify what one esteems;
when in an inferior
position, one can enlighten those not as good as oneself;
this is a sincere and generous *jūnzǐ*,
not yet reaching the level of the sage.
As for the laws of the hundred kings,
they are like distinguishing black from white;
responding to the changes of the age,
like counting the Three Bonds;
Observance of ritual requires regulation,
like the movement of the four limbs.
It is due to the transformative power,
like the progression of the four seasons.
The world then attains order,
and all creatures dwell in peace.
This is the mark of a sage.
The *Shī* [Book of Odes] says:
"Bright and radiant is the Zhōu [dynasty],
with regulations and order for those in office."
3.6 Wèi Wénhóu [魏文侯], wishing to appoint a prime minister,
summoned Lǐ Kè [李克] and asked him,
"I wish to appoint a prime minister;
either Dí Huáng [翟黃] or Wèi Chéngzi [魏成子].
I would like to consult you, sir."
Lǐ Kè [李克] left his mat and declined, saying,
"I have heard it said:
'The lowly do not deliberate on matters of the exalted;
those distant do not interfere in matters of the close.'
I am one who lives outside the court,
and dare not accept this commission."
Wénhóu [文侯] said,
"Sir, when faced with a task, do not decline."
Lǐ Kè [李克] said,
"Now, to observe a man,
when at leisure, observe those with whom he associates;
when rich, observe those with whom he shares;
when successful, observe those whom he promotes;
In poverty, observe what they do not do;
in destitution, observe what they do not take.
These five qualities are sufficient for observation."
Wén Hóu said,
"I invite you, Master, to take your residence.
My prime minister is decided."
Lǐ Kè went out and encountered Dí Huáng.
Dí Huáng said,
"Today I heard that you, sir, summoned the Master to divine the prime minister.
Who will it be?"
Lǐ Kè said,
"Wèi Chéngzǐ will be it."
Dí Huáng angrily changed his expression, saying,
"How have I wronged Wèi Chéngzǐ?
The governorship of Xī Hé
was what I recommended.
When you, sir, were worried about Yè,
I recommended Xīmén Bào.
When you, sir, wanted to attack Zhōngshān,
I recommended Yuè Yáng.
After Zhōngshān was captured,
and there was no one to defend it,
I recommended you, Master.
When you, sir, wanted to appoint a tutor for the crown prince,
I recommended Zhào Cāng.
All of them have had successes and accomplished tasks.
How have I wronged Wèi Chéngzǐ?"
Kè said,
"Your words are more effective than those of your lord,
how could you be compared to those who form cliques to seek high office?
When the ruler asked about appointing a prime minister,
it would either be Chéng (成) or Huáng (黃).
What do you think of these two men?"
The minister replied,
"Your lord does not understand the way to discern character.
When one is settled,
observe those they associate with;
when wealthy,
observe those they give to;
when successful,
observe those they promote;
when distressed,
observe what they will not do;
when poor,
observe what they will not take.
These five aspects are sufficient to determine a person's character,
why wait for them to be 'effective'?"
That is how I knew Wèi Chéngzǐ (魏成子) was fit to be prime minister.
Moreover, how can you compare yourself to Wèi Chéngzǐ?
Wèi Chéngzǐ's daily stipend is a thousand *zhōng* of grain,
one-tenth of which he uses personally,
to engage worthy men from all over the world.
This is how he obtained Bǔ Zǐxià (卜子夏), Tián Zǐfāng (田子方), and Duàn Gānmù (段干木).
These three men are all treated as teachers and friends by the ruler.
Those whom you recommend are all treated as subjects by the ruler.
How can you compare yourself to Wèi Chéngzǐ?"
Zhái Huáng hesitated, bowed again, and said:
"This humble person is ignorant
and has erred in his response to you, Master."
The *Shī* says:
"Bright and illustrious is the Zhōu,
its regulations and ranks are in order."
3.7 Lord Chéng, successor to the Duke,
was a ruler who gathered and calculated,
but did not yet reach the point of taking care of the people.
Zǐchǎn was one who took care of the people,
but did not yet reach the point of governing well.
Guǎn Zhòng governed well,
but did not yet reach the point of cultivating ritual.
Therefore, those who cultivate ritual become kings,
those who govern well become strong,
those who take care of the people attain peace,
and those who gather and calculate perish.
Therefore, to gather and calculate in order to attract grain,
and to accumulate wealth in order to enrich the enemy,
is the way to endanger oneself and destroy the state,
which an enlightened ruler will not tread.
He will cultivate ritual to harmonize the court,
rectify laws to regulate officials,
and equalize administration to benefit the common people.
Then, the rhythm will be harmonious in the court,
laws, rules, measures, and quantities will be correct among the officials,
and loyalty, trustworthiness, love, and punishment will be impartial among the common people.
In this way, the people will love him like their parents,
They feared him as they would spirits.
Therefore, his virtuous influence spread throughout the realm,
and blessings returned to the rulers and dukes.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Descend blessings abundantly,
Majestic is your demeanor.
Having drunk and eaten their fill,
Blessings and emoluments come repeatedly."
3.8 King Zhuāng of Chǔ was seriously ill.
They divined about it
and it was said:
"The River is causing trouble."
A high official said:
"Please use sacrificial animals."
King Zhuāng said:
"Stop!
The ancient sage kings established rules
that sacrifices should not exceed the bounds of what is hoped for [or within one's jurisdiction].
The Suī River, the Zhāng River, the Yángzi River, and the Hàn River
are within the bounds of Chǔ's jurisdiction.
Although I, the lonely one, am without virtue,
the River is not the place where I have committed offenses."
So he did not offer sacrifices.
After three days, his illness began to abate.
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) heard of it and said:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ's hegemony,
certainly had its methods!
He regulated extravagance and guarded his duty,
Turning inward and not being duplicitous,
isn't his hegemony fitting!"
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says,
"Alas, alas, protector and armor."
It refers to Zhuāng Wáng.
3.9 The illnesses of a ruler
manifest in twelve ways;
without a wise doctor,
none can be cured.
What are these twelve manifestations?
Atrophy, collapse, rebellion, bloating, fullness, diverging,
obstruction, blindness, vexation, panting, numbness, wind;
these are called the twelve manifestations.
How does a wise doctor cure them?
He says:
Reduce affairs and lighten punishments,
then atrophy will not arise.
Do not let the common people suffer hunger and cold,
then collapse will not arise.
Do not let wealth flow upwards,
then rebellion will not arise.
Do not let granaries accumulate rotten grain,
then bloating will not arise.
Do not let treasuries be filled to overflowing,
then fullness will not arise.
Do not let the ministers be unrestrained and indulgent,
then divergence will not arise.
Do not allow the sentiments of those below to fail to reach those above,
then *gé* (separation, alienation) will not arise.
If those of superior talent are concerned for those below,
then *huāng* (blindness, ignorance) will not arise.
If laws and orders are carried out,
then *fán* (trouble, vexation) will not arise.
Do not allow resentment to arise among those below,
then *chuǎn* (gasping, panting) will not arise.
Do not allow the worthy to remain hidden,
then *bì* (numbness, paralysis) will not arise.
Do not allow the common people to sing and chant criticisms,
then *fēng* (wind, discontent) will not arise.
Great ministers and the various subordinates
are the heart and limbs of the ruler.
If the heart and limbs are without illness,
then the ruler will be without illness.
Therefore, without a wise physician,
none can cure it.
If all people have these twelve ailments
and do not employ a wise physician,
then the state is not the state it should be.
The *Shī* [Book of Odes] says:
"When there are too many fiery and oppressive men,
there is no cure."
In the end, it will surely perish.
Therefore, if a wise physician is employed,
the masses will be without illness;
how much more so the ruler?
3.10 The *Zhuan* says:
In times of great peace,
there are no mutes or deaf people,
no cripples or the blind,
no dwarves or the lame,
no hunchbacks,
no people with broken or short limbs,
fathers do not weep for their sons,
elder brothers do not weep for their younger brothers,
and on the roads, there are no abandoned infants left in their swaddling clothes.
That everyone lives out their natural lifespan in order,
is due to the employment of worthy physicians.
Therefore, to ensure peace, stability, and normalcy,
the way to eliminate disease is nothing other than
employing worthy people.
The *Shi Jing* says:
"There are blind musicians, there are blind musicians,
in the court of Zhōu."
They are the remaining people of Zhòu (紂).
3.11 The *Zhuan* says:
If the rites of mourning and sacrifice are abandoned,
then the kindness between subjects and rulers will become thin.
If the kindness between subjects and rulers becomes thin,
then there will be many who turn their backs on death and embrace life.
The *Xiao Ya* says:
"May sons and grandsons,
not abandon to continue it."
3.12 When human affairs and moral principles are in accordance with the spirits,
when they are in accordance with the spirits,
then blessings will descend in great abundance.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"With offerings and sacrifices,
may we seek great blessings."
3.13 When Wǔ Wáng 武王 attacked Zhòu 紂,
he arrived at Xíngqiū 邢丘.
A shield broke into three pieces,
and it rained for three days without stopping.
Wǔ Wáng 武王 was afraid in his heart,
and summoned Tàigōng 太公 and asked him,
saying:
"Perhaps Zhòu 紂 is not yet ready to be attacked?"
Tàigōng 太公 replied,
"No.
The shield breaking into three pieces
means that the army should be divided into three.
The rain for three days without stopping
is meant to wash our weapons."
Wǔ Wáng 武王 said,
"Then what should be done?"
Tàigōng 太公 said,
"Love those people,
and even the crows on their roofs.
Hate those people,
and detest even their remnants.
Completely kill their enemies,
Do not allow them to have excess."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Alas!
The world is not yet settled."
Zhōu Gōng hastened forward and said:
"Not so.
Let each measure their dwelling,
and till their fields,
without regard to old or new possessions.
If the common people have transgressions,
let it rest with me alone."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Alas!
The world is already settled."
Then he drilled the army and rested the soldiers at Níng,
and renamed Xíng Qiū as Huái Níng,
calling it Xiū Wǔ,
because he conquered Zhòu at the Mu Fields.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"The Mu Fields are vast,
the sandalwood chariots are grand,
the teams of red-bay horses are surging.
It was Shī Shàngfù,
at this time, like an eagle soaring,
assisting that Wǔ Wáng,
to greatly attack the Great Shāng,
uniting in the clear morning."
Having returned from Shāng,
As soon as he alighted from the chariot,
he enfeoffed the descendants of the Yellow Emperor at Kuài,
he enfeoffed the descendants of Emperor Yáo at Zhù,
he enfeoffed the descendants of Shùn at Chén.
Immediately upon alighting from the chariot,
he enfeoffed the descendants of the Xià Dynasty rulers at Qǐ,
he enfeoffed the descendants of the Yīn Dynasty at Sòng,
he honored the grave of Bǐgān,
he released Jīzi from imprisonment,
he marked the neighborhood of Shāng Róng.
Crossing the river to the west,
he released the horses on the southern slopes of Mount Huà,
to show that he would not ride them again.
He released the oxen in the fields of Táolín,
to show that he would not yoke them again.
The chariots and armor were smeared with blood
and stored in the armory,
to show that they would not be used again.
Thereupon, he abolished the military and held suburban archery ceremonies;
shooting the "Líshǒu" to the left,
and shooting the "Zōuyú" to the right,
and then the world knew that King Wǔ would not use military force again.
By sacrificing at the Míngtáng, the people knew about filial piety;
by holding audiences, the feudal lords knew to show respect.
He seated the Three Elders in the Great Academy,
and the Son of Heaven held
the sauce and served them food,
held the goblet and offered them drink,
This is how to teach the feudal lords about fraternal duty.
These four things,
are the great teachings of the world.
Is it not fitting that the use of military force should not be prolonged?
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Having conquered the Yin and stopped the Liu,
you have secured your achievements."
This speaks of King Wǔ defeating Zhòu and the demise of the Yin dynasty.
3.14 Mèngcháng Jūn requested to study under Mǐn Zǐ,
and sent a carriage to welcome Mǐn Zǐ.
Mǐn Zǐ said:
"According to propriety, there is coming to learn, but not going to teach.
If one sends a teacher, and study cannot occur,
then going to teach will not be able to transform the ruler.
What the ruler considers impossible to learn,
the minister considers impossible to transform."
Thereupon Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"I respectfully receive your instructions."
The next day, he removed his fine robes and requested to receive instruction.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Daily advancing, monthly progressing."
3.15 Though a sword is sharp,
if it is not sharpened, it will not cut.
Though timber is fine,
if it is not studied, it will not reach great heights.
Though there is fine wine and delicious food,
if one does not taste it, one will not know its deliciousness.
Even if there is a good way,
if you don't learn, you won't attain its benefits.
Therefore, after learning, one knows one's own inadequacy;
after teaching, one knows one's own lack of thoroughness.
Because of inadequacy,
one feels ashamed and strives.
Because of a lack of thoroughness,
one exhausts the teachings of the master and becomes proficient.
Viewing it from this perspective,
then teaching and learning promote each other.
Zǐ Xià 子夏 asked about the *Book of Poetry*,
learning one thing and understanding two.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"The one who inspires me
is Shāng 商.
Now I can begin to discuss the *Book of Poetry* with him!"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 was superior to outstanding individuals and possessed complete sagely virtue,
his disciples were bathed in glory, and their virtue was evident.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Daily advance, monthly progress."
3.16 In all ways of learning,
a strict teacher is difficult (to find).
If the teacher is strict,
then the Way is revered.
If the Way is revered,
then the people know to respect learning.
Therefore, in the rites of the Imperial Academy,
even if addressed to the Emperor,
Not facing north
is to respect the teacher and value the Way.
Therefore, to be trusted without speaking,
and to be feared without anger,
that is what is meant by a teacher.
The *Book of Odes* says:
"Daily advancing, monthly progressing,
learning constantly achieves brilliance."
3.17 The *Commentary* says:
In Sòng there was a great flood.
The people of Lǔ sent condolences, saying:
"Heaven sent excessive rain,
harming the sacrificial millet,
extending to your territory,
causing worry for the ruling government,
so your servant respectfully sends condolences."
The people of Sòng responded, saying:
"I, the lonely one, am not benevolent,
my fasting and purification are not well practiced,
causing the people to not be timely.
Heaven has added calamity,
and also left you with worry.
I am shamed by the honor of your mandate."
Kǒngzǐ heard this
and said:
"The state of Sòng is perhaps close to being alright!"
The disciples asked:
"What do you mean?"
Confucius said:
"In the past, Jié and Zhòu did not acknowledge their mistakes,
so their downfall was sudden.
Chéng Tāng and Wén Wáng knew how to acknowledge their mistakes,
so their rise was swift.
To correct a mistake after making it
is not (really) making a mistake."
The people of Sòng heard this,
and so rose early and slept late,
offering condolences to the dead and inquiring after the sick,
and exerted their strength within the realm.
After three years,
the harvest was plentiful and the government was at peace.
Had the envoy from the countryside not heard the words of Confucius,
then the year's crops would not have been plentiful,
and the nation would not have been at peace.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Help me with my duties,
show me your manifest virtuous conduct."
3.18 Duke Huán of Qí set up torches in the courtyard,
to provide convenience for those who wished to be received in audience.
After a full year, scholars did not come.
Thereupon, a commoner from Dōngyě sought an audience using the art of multiplication tables.
Duke Huán made fun of him,
saying:
"Is multiplication tables enough to be received?"
The commoner said:
"I have heard that you set up torches in the courtyard to await scholars,
After a year, scholars did not arrive.
The reason why scholars did not arrive
is that you,
Your Majesty, are a virtuous ruler in the world.
Scholars from all directions believe themselves to be inferior to you,
and therefore do not come.
The "Nine-Nine" song
is only a trivial skill,
yet Your Majesty still treats it with respect.
How much more so should those who are more capable than the "Nine-Nine" be treated?
Mount Tài does not reject pebbles,
and rivers and seas do not refuse small streams;
this is how they achieve their greatness.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"The former people had a saying:
Consult with grass cutters and firewood gatherers,"
meaning to seek broad counsel."
Duke Huán said,
"Good."
So he strengthened his respectful treatment of them.
After a month,
scholars from all directions led each other to arrive.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"From the hall to the foundation,
from the sheep to the ox."
Accomplish great things from small beginnings.
3.19 In times of great peace,
the people performing corvée labor do not exceed the allotted time,
Men and women do not miss the proper time to pair up;
Filial sons do not miss the proper time to provide for their parents.
Externally, there are no unmarried men;
Internally, there are no resentful women.
Above, there are no fathers who are not kind;
Below, there are no sons who are not filial.
Fathers and sons complement each other;
Husbands and wives protect each other.
The world is peaceful;
The state is tranquil.
Human affairs are well-prepared below;
The Dao of Heaven responds above.
Therefore, Heaven does not change its constant principles;
Earth does not alter its form;
The sun and moon shine brightly;
The constellations follow their regular paths.
Heaven bestows and Earth transforms;
*Yīn* and *Yáng* are in harmonious union;
Movement is manifested in thunder and lightning;
Moisture is provided by wind and rain;
Regulation is achieved by mountains and rivers;
Cold and heat are balanced.
All people are nurtured and grow;
Each obtains their proper place;
And (this allows one to) control the state's resources.
Therefore, the state has something to rely on for stability;
The land has someone to be its master.
Sages hollowed out wood to make boats;
Carving wood to make oars
to facilitate the flow of goods from all directions,
enabling the people of the marshes to have enough water,
and the people of the mountains to have enough fish,
so that surplus wealth can circulate.
Thus, the rich lands do not rejoice alone,
and the barren lands do not suffer alone.
Even if they encounter years of famine and hardship,
such as the great floods of Yǔ (禹) and droughts of Tāng (湯),
the people will not have the appearance of being frozen or starving.
Thus, the living will not lack resources,
and the dead will not have their corpses exposed.
This is what is meant by happiness.
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
"Oh, shining is the royal army,
following the way of nourishing in times of obscurity."
3.20 One who can govern the world,
must be able to nourish its people.
One who can nourish the people,
is nourishing oneself.
Diet suits the organs,
flavors suit the qi,
work and rest suit the muscles and bones,
cold and warmth suit the skin,
then the qi of the organs is balanced,
the mind is governed,
thoughts are correct,
joy and anger are timely,
In daily life, he rises, rests, and enjoys himself;
in dealing with affairs, he acts according to the season and uses his resources appropriately.
This is what is meant by being able to nourish oneself.
Therefore, the sage does not indulge in excessive pleasure, extravagance, or wastefulness.
It is not because he despises beauty and loves wealth.
Nourishment has its proper measure;
excess leads to unhappiness;
therefore, he does not do it.
Therefore, he does not bathe frequently in summer;
it is not because he cherishes water.
He does not often soak in hot water in winter;
it is not because he cherishes fire.
He does not build high terraces and pavilions;
it is not because he lacks earth and wood.
He does not cast large bells and tripods;
it is not because he lacks metal and tin.
He does not drown himself in wine,
nor is he greedy for beauty;
it is not because he shuns ugliness.
He simply follows the ease of his emotions and nature,
and his system can become a model for the world.
Therefore, his use of resources does not waste wealth,
but is sufficient to nourish his life,
and the world praises his benevolence (rén).
His nourishment does not harm his nature,
but is sufficient to establish teachings,
and the world praises his righteousness (yì).
He adapts to his emotions and avoids excess,
He does not seek what is not rightfully his,
and the world praises his incorruptibility.
Established deeds cannot be concealed,
cessation of punishment cannot be violated,
adhering to one principle and holding all things lightly,
the world praises his courage.
These four virtues reside in the people:
in repose, they are gentle and pleasing;
in anger, they overcome the enemy.
Therefore, examine the means by which they are nurtured, and the tools for governance will be complete.
With the tools for governance complete, those near and far will be nurtured.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Oh, shining is the royal army,
conforming to nourishment and biding its time."
This speaks of mutual nourishment leading to obscurity.
3.21 Gōngyí Xiū was the prime minister of Lǔ and had a fondness for fish.
The people of the state all offered him fish, but he did not accept them.
His younger brother admonished him, saying:
"You are fond of fish but do not accept them,
why is this?"
He replied:
"It is precisely because I am fond of fish
that I do not accept them.
If I accept fish and am dismissed from my position as prime minister,
then I will not be able to provide myself with fish.
If I do not accept them and am not dismissed from my position as prime minister,
then I will be able to provide myself with fish for a long time."
This is clear in the case of the fish acting for itself.
Therefore, the *Lǎozǐ* says:
"Place the self last, and the self comes first;
place the self outside, and the self is preserved.
Is it not because of its selflessness
that it can achieve its self-interest?"
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Thoughts without evil."
This is what it refers to.
3.22 The *Zhuàn* (Commentary) says:
In Lǔ, there was a father and son who were in litigation;
Kāngzǐ wanted to execute them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"They cannot be executed yet.
The fact that the people are litigating, father against son, shows that unrighteousness has existed for a long time.
This means that those above have lost their way.
If those above had the Way,
this person would be dead (i.e., such a thing would not happen)."
The litigant heard this
and requested to drop the lawsuit.
Kāngzǐ said:
"Governing the people with filial piety,
killing one unrighteous person to punish those who are unfilial,
would that not be permissible?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No.
To listen to their lawsuits without teaching them,
To kill the innocent is wrong.
If the entire army suffers a great defeat,
it is not right to punish them.
If judicial cases are not handled properly,
it is not right to inflict punishment.
If the teachings of the ruler are clearly presented and he first adheres to them himself,
then the people will follow like the wind.
If he personally practices these teachings and the people still do not follow,
only then should he subject them to punishments,
so that the people will understand their offenses.
Now, a wall one *rèn* tall,
the people cannot climb over,
but a mountain a hundred *rèn* tall,
even young children climb and play on it,
because the incline is gradual.
Now, the gradual decline of benevolence and righteousness has been going on for a long time.
Can it be said that the people will not overstep (the bounds)?
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"So that the people are not led astray."
The noble men of old
guided their people so as not to mislead them,
and therefore, though they possessed stern authority, they did not test it,
and punishments were set aside and not used.
Therefore, make evident your benevolence and righteousness,
be meticulous in your teachings and guidance,
cause the people to see it clearly with their eyes,
cause the people to hear it distinctly with their ears,
cause the people to understand it lucidly in their hearts,
Then the Way will not be confusing, and the people's minds will not be deluded.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"Show us manifest virtuous conduct."
Therefore, if the principles of the Way and righteousness are not easily changed,
the people will not deviate.
If rites and music are not clear,
the people will not see them.
The *Shī* says:
"The road of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
its straightness like an arrow,"
speaking of its easiness.
"Where the gentleman treads,
the common man watches,"
speaking of its clarity.
"Turning our heads to look at it,
tears flow down,"
lamenting that they did not hear of rites and teachings, and thus are subjected to punishments.
To neglect fundamental teachings and then wait for punishment,
is like breaking open the cage and shooting with poisoned arrows;
is that not sad?
Therefore, it is said that they should not be killed yet.
Formerly, the former kings guided the people with rites,
which can be compared to driving a chariot.
Punishments
are like whips and prods.
It is like driving a horse without bridle and bit, only with whips and prods.
If you want the horse to advance,
you whip its rear;
If you want a horse to retreat,
you whip its front.
The driver becomes exhausted and the horse is greatly injured.
It is just like this now.
The ruler is troubled and weary, and the people frequently suffer punishment.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"If a man has no *lǐ* (ritual propriety),
why does he not quickly die?"
If the ruler is without *lǐ*,
then he will not avoid calamity.
If the subordinate is without *lǐ*,
then he will not avoid punishment.
If both ruler and subordinate are without *lǐ*,
why do they not quickly die?"
Kāngzǐ (康子), rising from his mat, bowed twice and said:
"Although I am not clever,
I will remember these words."
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) withdrew from the court,
and his disciple Zǐlù (子路) challenged him, saying:
"Is it right for a father and son to sue each other?"
Is this the *dào* (the way)?
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
"No, it is not."
Zǐlù (子路) said:
"In that case, why did you, Master, being a *jūnzǐ* (gentleman), dismiss the case?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
"To not give warning and then demand completion is harmful.
[This is a] *hài* (harm).
To delay commands and then punish for tardiness
is tyrannical.
To execute without prior instruction
is thievery.
A gentleman in government
avoids these three.
Moreover, the *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Bearing a pleased countenance and a smile,
It is not in anger, but in teaching."
3.23 During the time of Shùn,
the Miáo people did not submit.
The reason they did not submit
was that Mount Héng was in the south,
and Mount Qí was in the north,
with the waves of Dòngtíng Lake on the left,
and the waters of Péngzé Lake on the right,
making it a strategically dangerous location.
Because they did not submit,
Yǔ requested to attack them,
but Shùn did not permit it,
saying:
"My explanations and teachings have not yet been exhausted."
After prolonged explanations and teachings,
the Miáo people requested to submit.
The world heard of this,
and all belittled the righteousness of Yǔ,
and praised the virtue of Shùn.
The *Shī* says:
"Bearing a cheerful countenance and a smile,
not with anger, but with instruction."
This speaks of Shùn.
Someone asked:
"In that case, does Yǔ's virtue not reach that of Shùn?"
I replied:
"That is not so.
The reason why Yǔ requested to undertake punitive expeditions
was to manifest Shùn's virtue.
Therefore, when there was good, he praised the ruler;
when there was fault, he blamed himself.
This is the proper conduct of a subject.
Supposing Yǔ were the ruler
and Shùn were the subject,
it would be just the same as this.
Truly, Yǔ can be said to have thoroughly understood the great principles of being a subject."
3.24 Jì Sūnzi was governing Lǔ,
executing many people and invariably getting their crimes right,
punishing many people and invariably getting their faults right.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"How tyrannical is this governing!" Jì Sūn heard this and
said:
"I execute people and invariably get their crimes right,
punish people and invariably get their faults right;
the Master thinks it is tyrannical, why is that?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Why not be like Zǐchǎn's governance of Zhèng?
In one year, the offenses deserving punishment were reduced;
in two years, the crimes deserving execution vanished;
in three years, the prisons were empty of prisoners.
Therefore, the people returned to him as water flows downward,
loved him as filial sons respect their parents.
When Zǐchǎn 子產 was sick and about to die,
the people of the state all sighed and said:
"Who can we find to die in place of Zǐchǎn?"
When he could not avoid death,
the officers and gentlemen wept for him in the court,
the merchants wept for him in the marketplace,
the farmers wept for him in the fields.
Those who wept for Zǐchǎn
all grieved as if they had lost their parents.
Now, I have heard that when you, Master, are ill,
the people of the state rejoice;
when you recover, the people of the state are all terrified.
They congratulate each other on your death,
and fear each other on your recovery.
What is this if not tyranny?
I, Cì 賜, have heard that
governing by relying on the law is called tyranny;
setting a deadline without warning is called cruelty;
executing without teaching is called robbery;
conquering people with one's own strength is called oppression.
The oppressor loses himself;
the robber loses his subjects;
the cruel one loses his government;
Tyrants lose the people.
Furthermore, I have heard that if one occupying a high position acts in these four ways and does not perish, such a thing has never happened."
Thereupon, Jìsūn bowed his head and apologized, saying:
"I respectfully receive your instructions."
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Bearing cheerful looks, bearing smiles,
Not anger, but instruction."
3.25 The questioner said:
"Why do the wise find pleasure in water?"
He replied:
"Water follows principles in its course,
Leaving no small space untouched,
Resembling the wise.
Moving downward,
Resembling the polite.
Treading deep without hesitation,
Resembling the brave.
Hindered and defended, yet clear,
Resembling those who understand destiny.
Passing through danger to reach afar,
Ultimately succeeding without being destroyed,
Resembling those with virtue.
Heaven and earth are completed by it,
Myriad things are brought to life by it,
The state is pacified by it, all affairs are leveled by it,
All things are rectified by it.
This is why the wise find pleasure in water."
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Sī lè pàn shuǐ,
bó cǎi qí máo.
Lǔ hóu lì zhǐ,
zài pàn yǐn jiǔ."
This speaks of delighting in water.
3.26 A questioner asked:
"Why do the benevolent delight in mountains?"
The answer was:
"Mountains are what all people look up to.
Grasses and trees grow there,
all things are planted there,
flying birds gather there,
running beasts rest there,
and the four quarters obtain benefits from them.
Clouds emerge and the wind travels, reaching between heaven and earth.
Heaven and earth are thereby completed,
and the state is thereby pacified.
This is why the benevolent delight in mountains."
The *Shī* says:
"Tài Shān is lofty,
what the state of Lǔ looks up to."
This speaks of delighting in mountains.
3.27 The *Zhuàn* says:
When Duke Wén of Jìn once fled into exile and then returned to his state,
he distributed rewards three times, but did not include Táo Shūhú.
Táo Shūhú said to Jiù Fàn:
"I followed you in exile for eleven years,
my complexion darkened,
my hands and feet calloused.
Now that you have returned to the state and distributed rewards three times, I have not received any.
Have you forgotten me?
Or have I committed a great offense?
Please, speak to me about it."
Jiù Fàn spoke of this to Wén Gōng,
Wén Gōng said:
"Ah!
How could I forget this man?
One of high intelligence and supreme virtue,
whose will and actions are wholly accomplished,
who steeped me in the Dao,
persuaded me with benevolence,
transformed my conduct,
enlightened me,
and made me a complete man—
I consider this the highest reward.
One who respects me with ritual,
protects me with righteousness,
is my bulwark and support,
and prevents me from doing wrong—
I consider this the next highest.
One who is brave, fierce, and militarily strong,
whose spirit commands himself,
who places himself in the front when danger is ahead,
and places himself in the rear when danger is behind,
To deliver me from danger and difficulty,
I consider to be secondary.
But those who toil diligently deserve even lower consideration."
The *Shī* says:
"Walking cautiously, never exceeding;
Following sights that have already been observed."
Now, if one does not internally reflect on one's own faults,
and does not please the common people,
with what will one be rewarded?
3.28 Those who deceive others say:
"The circumstances of ancient and modern times are different;
therefore, the ways of governing order and chaos are different.
And the masses are all foolish and ignorant,
shallow and without measure."
Even in what they see before their eyes, they can be deceived;
how much more so after a thousand years?
These deceivers,
even within their own household, still harbor deceit,
how much more so concerning matters a thousand years prior?
In that case, how is it that the sage cannot be deceived?
I say:
The sage measures others by himself.
He measures hearts by hearts,
feelings by feelings,
kinds by kinds.
Ancient and modern times are the same.
If categories do not contradict each other,
then the principles remain the same, even after a long time.
Therefore, nature aligns with principle and is not deluded.
Before the Five Emperors, there were no transmissions of people.
It was not that there were no worthy people,
But it was due to the length of time.
Among the Five Emperors, there were no transmissions of governance.
It was not that there was no good governance,
But it was due to the length of time.
The Yú and Xià dynasties had transmissions of governance,
But they were not as detailed as those of the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties.
It was not that there was no good governance,
But it was due to the length of time.
Now, transmissions become more abbreviated the longer they are,
And more detailed the closer they are.
Abbreviated transmissions emphasize the big picture,
Detailed transmissions emphasize the finer points.
Therefore, the foolish person hears about the big picture but does not understand the finer points,
And hears about the finer points but does not understand the big picture.
This is why there are discrepancies over time.
The Three Kings and Five Emperors
Represented the peak of governance.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"The decrees of the Emperor are not disobeyed,
Reaching to Tāng Qí."
Saying that ancient and modern times are the same.
3.29 Shùn was born in Zhū Féng,
Moved to Fù Xià,
And died in Míng Tiáo,
He was a man of the Eastern Barbarians.
King Wén (Wén Wáng) was born in Qízhōu,
and died in Bìyǐng.
He was a man of the Western Yi people.
The distance between the places
is more than a thousand *lǐ*,
and the distance between the times is more than a thousand years,
yet he achieved his ambitions and his way was practiced in the Central Kingdom,
as if matching tallies.
Confucius said:
"Former sages and later sages,
their principles are the same."
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"The decree of the Lord is not violated,
reaching to Tāng's equality."
3.30 Confucius observed a tilting vessel in the Zhōu temple.
There was a tilting vessel.
Confucius asked the temple guard,
"What is this vessel called?"
He replied,
"This is called a vessel to be placed beside one's seat."
Confucius said,
"I have heard that the vessel beside one's seat overturns when full,
overturns when full,
leans when empty,
and is upright when in the middle.
Is this so?"
He replied,
"Yes."
Confucius sent Zilu to fetch water and test it.
When full, it overturns;
when half-full, it stands upright;
when empty, it leans.
Confucius sighed and said,
"Alas!
How can there be something full that does not overturn!"
Zilu said,
"May I venture to ask if there is a way to maintain fullness?"
Confucius said,
"The way to maintain fullness
is to suppress and diminish it."
Zilu said,
"Is there a way to diminish it?"
Confucius said,
"Those whose virtue is generous
should guard it with respect.
Those whose land is vast
should guard it with frugality.
Those whose rank and position are exalted
should guard it with humility.
Those whose people are numerous and soldiers are strong
should guard it with awe.
Those who are intelligent and wise
should guard it with foolishness.
Those who are widely learned and have a strong memory
should guard it with shallowness.
This is what is meant by suppressing and diminishing it."
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
"[Tāng](湯)'s descent was not slow,
His sage reverence daily increased."
3.31 Duke Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng 周公) held the position of the Son of Heaven for seven years.
Among commoners in simple clothes, those who held gifts as a sign of respect and were seen by him as teachers numbered ten.
Those he befriended and met numbered twelve.
Those first seen in impoverished alleys and humble dwellings numbered forty-nine.
Those who were regularly promoted for their goodness numbered a hundred.
Those taught as scholars numbered a thousand.
Those who attended the court numbered ten thousand.
When King Chéng (Chéng Wáng 成王) enfeoffed Bó Qín (伯禽) in Lǔ (魯),
Duke Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng 周公) warned him, saying:
"Go!
