Do not use the state of Lǔ (魯) to act arrogantly towards scholars.
I am the son of King Wén (Wén Wáng 文王),
the younger brother of King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng 武王),
and the uncle of King Chéng (Chéng Wáng 成王).
Moreover, I assist the Son of Heaven.
In the world, I am not unimportant.
Yet, I would clasp my hair three times after one wash,
and spit out my food three times during one meal,
still fearing to lose the scholars of the world.
I have heard that when virtue and conduct are broad and generous,
if one guards them with respect,
one will be honored.
When land is vast and extensive,
if one guards it with frugality,
one will be secure.
To hold high rank and great emolument
with humility is
noble.
To hold numerous people and strong soldiers
with awe is
to be victorious.
To hold intelligence and sagacity
with apparent foolishness is
good.
To hold vast knowledge and strong memory
with the appearance of shallowness is
wise.
These six things
are all virtues of humility.
To be noble as the Son of Heaven [Tiānzǐ],
and rich with all that the four seas contain,
is due to these virtues.
Those who were not humble and lost the empire and their lives,
such as Jié [Jié] and Zhòu [Zhòu],
must be regarded with caution!
Therefore, the *Book of Changes* (*Yì*) has a principle:
great enough to preserve the empire,
moderate enough to preserve the state,
and near enough to preserve oneself.
It is called humility.
The Way of Heaven diminishes fullness and benefits humility;
the Way of Earth transforms fullness and flows towards humility;
ghosts and spirits harm fullness and bless humility;
People say to detest fullness and to like humility.
Therefore, when clothes are made, there must be a missing edge;
when a palace is built, there must be a missing corner;
when a house is completed, clumsiness must be added.
Showing incompleteness
is the way of Heaven.
The *Yì*
says, "Humility brings success;
the superior person has a good end."
The *Shī*
says, "Tāng descended not slowly;
with reverence, his virtue daily ascended."
Take heed!
Let there be no one in the Lǔ 魯 state who is proud of his position."
3.32 The *Zhuàn* says:
Zǐlù 子路, dressed in elaborate clothes, went to see Kǒngzǐ 孔子.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said,
"Yóu 由, what is this laxity?
In the past, the Jiāng 江 River at Wèn 汶,
when it first began,
was not enough to fill a cup.
But when it reaches the mouth of the Jiāng 江 River,
without boats,
without avoiding the wind,
it cannot be crossed.
Is this not due to the multitude of streams?
Now, your clothes are extravagant,
your expression is full of pride,
"Who in the world could surpass you?"
Zǐ Lù hurried out,
changed his clothes, and re-entered,
appearing properly respectful.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, remember this.
Let me tell you.
Those who are careful in their words do not clamor,
those who are careful in their actions do not boast.
To pretend to know something based on appearance and to consider oneself superior is the mark of a petty person.
Therefore, a *jūnzǐ* acknowledges what he knows as knowing,
and acknowledges what he does not know as not knowing—
this is the key to speech.
To acknowledge what one is capable of as being capable,
and to acknowledge what one is incapable of as being incapable—
this is the key to action.
If speech is essential, one is wise;
if action is essential, one is benevolent.
Having both wisdom and benevolence,
what more could be added?
The *Shī* says:
'Tāng's descent was not delayed;
His sage reverence daily ascended.'"
3.33 A *jūnzǐ*'s actions are not valued for being recklessly difficult,
his words are not valued for being recklessly astute,
his reputation is not valued for being recklessly spread;
only what is appropriate is valued.
To carry a stone and jump into a river
What is difficult to do,
Shēntú Dí was able to do it.
What the junzi does not value
is that which is not in accordance with propriety and righteousness.
Mountains and abysses being level,
heaven and earth being side by side,
the states of Qí and Qín attacking each other,
entering the ear,
exiting the mouth,
hooks having beards,
eggs having hair—
these are sayings difficult to maintain,
but Dèng Xī and Huì Shī were able to maintain them.
What the junzi does not value
is that which is not in accordance with propriety and righteousness.
Even if Zhí, the robber, chants,
his reputation will be like the sun and moon,
passed down with Shùn and Yǔ without ceasing.
What the junzi does not value
is that which is not in accordance with propriety and righteousness.
Therefore, the junzi values not doing what is simply difficult,
values not sayings that are simply penetrating,
values not reputations that are simply passed down,
but values that which is appropriate.
The *Book of Poetry* says,
"Neither competing nor demanding,
neither rigid nor yielding."
3.34 Bó Yí and Shū Qí did not look upon evil sights
Ears do not listen to evil sounds.
He does not serve a ruler who is not his own;
he does not employ people who are not his own.
Where tyrannical government originates,
where tyrannical people reside,
he cannot bear to live.
He desires to live among the villagers,
as if wearing court robes and a court hat,
sitting in mud and charcoal.
Therefore, those who hear of Bó Yí's 伯夷 example,
greedy men become honest,
and cowardly men develop resolute will.
As for Liǔ Xià Huì 柳下惠, it is not so.
He is not ashamed to serve a corrupt ruler,
nor does he decline a petty office.
When advancing, he does not conceal the worthy;
he must follow the proper path.
In hardship and poverty, he does not grieve;
though lost and neglected, he does not complain.
Living among the villagers,
he is cheerful and unwilling to leave.
Even if someone were to strip naked beside me,
how could they sully me?
Therefore, those who hear of Liǔ Xià Huì's 柳下惠 example,
vulgar men become tolerant,
and unkind men become generous.
As for Kǒngzǐ 孔子 leaving Lǔ 魯,
he departed slowly,
To be able to leave and then leave,
to be able to stop and then stop,
that is the way to leave one's parents' country.
Bó Yí,
is the pure one among sages.
Liǔxià Huì,
is the harmonious one among sages.
Kǒngzǐ,
is the central one among sages.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Neither contend nor strive,
neither be rigidly strong nor softly weak."
This is what is meant by moderation, harmony, and universal understanding.
3.35 The king's
equitable imposition of government duties:
in the fields and wilderness, one tenth (tax);
at the passes and markets, inspect but do not levy;
the mountains, forests, marshes and weirs,
allow entry according to the seasons and do not prohibit.
Assess the land and regulate the soil.
Manage the paths and cause tribute to arrive.
The myriad things come in groups,
without anything being stagnant,
in order to communicate and move with each other,
those nearby do not conceal their abilities,
those far away do not resent their labor,
even secluded and remote countries,
None did not hasten to serve him and found peace and joy in it.
This is what is called a king's
equal distribution of burdens and correct affairs.
The *Shī* says:
"He spreads his government with ease and grace,
And all blessings come flowing in."
3.36 Sūn Qīng and the Lord of Línwǔ discussed military affairs before King Xiàochéng of Zhao.
The King said:
"May I venture to ask about the essentials of warfare?"
The Lord of Línwǔ said:
"The essentials of warfare are
that superiors obtain the opportune time of heaven,
inferiors obtain the advantages of the terrain,
one moves after the opponent,
and arrives before the opponent.
These are the essentials of warfare."
Sūn Qīng said:
"That is not so.
The essentials of warfare
lie in attaching and cherishing the officers and common people.
If the six horses are not in harmony,
Zàofù cannot make them go far.
If the bow and arrows are not properly adjusted,
Yì cannot hit subtle targets.
If the officers and common people are not close and attached,
Tāng and Wǔ cannot win battles.
From this point of view,
the essential lies in attaching and cherishing the officers and common people."
Lín Wǔ Jūn said:
"That's not right.
The use of soldiers
lies in adapting to changing circumstances.
What is valued
is strategy and deception.
Those who are good at using them are like a fleeing rabbit,
no one knows where it will emerge from.
Sūn Wú used them and had no equal in the world.
Judging from this,
how can one say that it is necessary to wait for the affection of the officers and people before being able to succeed?"
Sūn Qīng said:
"That's not right.
What you are talking about
is the army of feudal lords
and the affairs of strategists.
What I am talking about
is the army of the benevolent
and the affairs of the sage kings.
Those who can be deceived
must be negligent.
The relationship between ruler and subject, superiors and inferiors
must have a stark departure from virtue.
If Zhí were to deceive Jié,
there would still be skill and clumsiness involved.
But if Jié were to deceive Yáo,
it would be like stirring boiling water with a finger,
throwing an egg at a stone,
To embrace feathers and rush into raging fire
, one will only burn one's ears upon entering.
How can this be deceived?
Moreover, with whom will a tyrannical state arrive?
Those with whom it arrives must be those who deceive its people.
The people are intimate with me,
fragrant like pepper and orchids,
joyful like fathers and sons.
They regard their superiors
as if they were venomous wasps and scorpions.
Human nature is such that
even Jié and Zhí would not willingly do what their people hate,
or harm what their people love most.
This is like making one's children harm their own parents.
They will be the first to realize the error;
how can this be deceived?
Furthermore, the troops of a benevolent person
, when gathered, form units;
when scattered, they form ranks.
Extended, they are like the long blade of Móyé
, those who encounter it are cut.
Sharpened, they are like the sharp point of Móyé
, those who face it collapse.
When they are arranged in a circle, they are like hills and mountains that cannot be moved;
when they are arranged in a square, they are like a large rock that cannot be uprooted.
Those who touch them will have their horns and joints broken and be forced to retreat.
How can this be deceived?
The *Book of Odes* says:
"King Wǔ carried the banner,
with reverence holding the battle-axe.
Like a blazing fire,
none would dare to resist us."
This refers to the armies of Tāng and Wǔ."
King Xiào Chéng, rising from his mat and looking up, said,
"Although I am not intelligent,
I will follow the methods of warfare of the Master."
3.37 A man who receives a mandate
stands upright, properly attired,
appearing dignified, inspiring hope, and earning trust.
Next is he who
is trusted upon hearing his words.
Next is he who
is trusted upon seeing his actions.
But if, after seeing his actions,
the people still do not trust him,
then he is the lowest.
The *Shī* says:
"Be careful of your words,
lest people not believe you."
3.38 In the past, without going out of the door, one could know the world;
without peeping through the window, one could see the way of Heaven.
It was not that the eyes could see a thousand *lǐ* ahead,
nor that the ears could hear a thousand *lǐ* away,
but that one used one's own
feelings to gauge it.
If one hates hunger and cold,
Then one knows that the world desires clothing and food.
One dislikes labor and hardship,
then one knows that the world desires ease and comfort.
One dislikes decline and weakness,
then one knows that the world desires wealth and abundance.
Knowing these three things,
is how the sage-kings rectified the world without descending from their mats.
Therefore, the way of the noble person
is nothing more than zhōng shù (忠恕, loyalty and empathy).
To be in a state of hunger and thirst, suffering one's blood and breath,
afflicted by cold and heat, moving one's muscles and skin,
these four things are the great harms of the people.
If these harms are not removed,
they cannot be taught and governed.
If the four limbs are not covered (with clothing),
then there are few rén rén (仁人, benevolent people).
If the five viscera are empty and weak,
then there will be no independent scholars.
Therefore, the law of the former kings
was that the Son of Heaven personally plowed,
and the empress personally engaged in silkworm cultivation,
being the first in the world to worry about clothing and food.
The *Shī* (詩, Book of Poetry) says:
"What have my parents ever spared?"
"My heart is filled with sorrow,
because my child has no clothes."
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, Scroll Four
4.1 Zhòu (紂) created the torture of the heated bronze pillar.
Prince Bǐ Gān (比干) said:
"To not remonstrate with a tyrannical ruler
is not loyalty.
To fear death and not speak
is not courage.
To remonstrate when one sees a fault,
and to die if one is not heeded,
is the height of loyalty."
Thereupon he remonstrated,
and for three days did not leave the court.
Zhòu (紂) imprisoned and killed him.
The *Shī* (詩, Book of Poetry) says:
"Vast and terrible is August Heaven,
I am careful to harm no innocent one."
4.2 Jié (桀) made a wine pool
large enough to sail a boat,
and a mound of wine dregs large enough to be seen from ten *lǐ* (里),
at one drumbeat, three thousand people drank like cattle.
Guān Lóngpáng (關龍逄) advanced to remonstrate, saying:
"The ancient rulers
personally practiced ritual propriety and righteousness,
loved the people, and conserved resources,
therefore their states were secure and they themselves lived long.
Now you, Sire, use wealth as if it were inexhaustible,
and kill people as if you feared you could not overcome them.
If you, Sire, do not reform,
heavenly calamities will certainly descend,
and punishment would certainly arrive.
Your lord should reform it."
He stood but did not leave the court.
Jié imprisoned and killed him.
A gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"It is the decree of Heaven."
The *Shī* [Poetry] says:
"Oh Vast Heaven, all-embracing!
I cautiously hold to those who are innocent."
4.3 There are those with great loyalty,
those with secondary loyalty,
those with lesser loyalty,
and those who are traitors to the state.
To cover the ruler with the Way and transform him,
this is called great loyalty.
To regulate the ruler with virtue and assist him,
this is called secondary loyalty.
To remonstrate against the ruler’s faults and incur his resentment,
this is called lesser loyalty.
To not care about the realization of public justice and righteousness,
to steal agreement and shamelessly concur in order to maintain one's salary and cultivate relationships,
this is called being a traitor to the state.
If one considers the Dān Zhōu Gōng's 周公 behavior toward Chéng Wáng 成王,
it can be called great loyalty.
Guǎn Zhòng's 管仲 behavior toward Huán Gōng 桓公,
can be called secondary loyalty.
Zǐ Xū's 子胥 behavior toward Fūchāi 夫差,
can be called lesser loyalty.
Cáo Chùlóng's actions towards Zhòu
can be described as those of a national traitor.
These are all the actions of subjects;
they are the effects of fortune and misfortune, virtue and lack thereof.
The *Shī* says:
"They do not merely attend to their duties,
but only seek to oppress the King."
4.4 Duke Āi asked about selecting men.
Confucius said:
"Do not select the overly strong,
do not select the flattering,
do not select those who are slanderous with their mouths.
Strength
is arrogance.
Flattery
is adulation.
Slander
is falsehood.
Therefore, first tune the bow,
and then seek strength in it.
First train the horse,
and then seek goodness in it.
First ensure that the scholar is trustworthy and sincere,
and then seek knowledge in him.
If a scholar is untrustworthy and yet very knowledgeable,
it is like a jackal or wolf,
it is difficult to approach him."
The *Zhōu Shū* says,
To add wings to a tiger,
is it not perilous?
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"It is not that they cease their contributions,
but only the king is distressed."
It speaks of those who are not respectful of their duties,
and worry their lord.
4.5 Duke Huán of Qí (Qí Huán Gōng) planned to attack Jǔ (Jǔ) alone with Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) counsel,
yet the people of the state knew of it.
Duke Huán said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I spoke only to you, Master Zhong (仲父),
yet the people of the state know of it. How is this?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Perhaps there is a sage in the state?
Where is Dōngguō Yá (東郭牙) now?"
Duke Huán looked around and said:
"He is here."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Did you say anything?"
Dōngguō Yá said:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"How did you know of it?"
He said:
"I have heard that a noble person has three complexions,
and that is how I knew of it."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"What are the three appearances (sān sè)?"
He replied:
"Joyful delight and loving speech are the appearances of bells and drums (zhōng gǔ zhī sè)."
(Repeated for clarity.)
"Melancholy and sorrow are the appearances of mourning garments (shuāi dié zhī sè)."
(Repeated for clarity.)
"Fierce intensity and full substance are the appearances of weapons and armor (bīng gé zhī sè)."
(Repeated for clarity.)
"This is how one knows them."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"How do you know it is Jǔ?"
He replied:
"The ruler faces southeast and points,
his mouth is open and not covered,
his tongue is raised and not lowered,
this is how one knows it is Jǔ."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent."
The *Book of Poetry* (*Shī*) says:
"Other men have minds,
I can surmise them."
Dōngguō Xiānshēng said:
"The eyes are the symbol of the heart.
Words are
the indicators of actions.
The wise man's understanding of others
never requires him to seek knowledge before being able to know.
By observing appearances,
Observe their spirit and will,
determine what to take and what to discard,
and human nature is completely understood."
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Other people have minds,
I surmise them."
4.6 Now, having strong armor and sharp weapons,
is not enough to deploy against the enemy and conquer the captives;
having good bows and well-tuned arrows,
is not enough to shoot far and hit small targets;
it is the same as having no army.
Having people, but not being able to use them strongly to resist enemies,
is the same as having no people.
Therefore, thousands of *lǐ* of flat rock
do not constitute having land;
millions of ignorant people
do not constitute having people.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"In the south is the winnowing basket,
which cannot be used for tossing grain.
In the north is the Dipper,
which cannot be used for ladling wine."
4.7 The *Commentary* says:
Shùn played a five-stringed zither,
and sang the poem "Southern Wind,"
and the world was governed.
Duke Píng of Zhōu did not part with wine in front of him,
and bells and chimes were always hung,
And the realm within [the four seas] was also well governed.
The common man with his hundred *mǔ* of land and one house,
has no time for leisure,
nor place to move to.
Now, if one person tries to listen to everything under Heaven,
his day will have time to spare, but governance will be insufficient.
This is to make people do it for him.
Now, if one monopolizes the power to employ people,
but cannot control the masses below,
then the one in office is not the right person.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"In the south, there is the winnowing basket,
but it cannot be used for winnowing.
In the north, there is the Dipper,
but it cannot be used for ladling wine."
It speaks of having the position but not the ability.
4.8 Duke Huán of Qí attacked the Shān Róng,
and on his way, he passed through Yān.
The ruler of Yān escorted him out of his territory.
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng, saying:
"When feudal lords escort each other,
is it proper to go out of the territory?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"One does not go out of the territory except for the Son of Heaven."
Duke Huán said:
"In that case, the ruler of Yān was fearful and lost his propriety.
I cannot allow Yān to lose its propriety."
Then he ceded the land reached by the Yān 君 (Yān Jūn) to him.
When the other feudal lords heard of this, they all paid court to Qí.
The *Shī* says:
"Reverently hold your position,
Love what is upright.
The spirits will listen to you,
And grant you great blessings."
4.9 The *Sháo* using shields and axes,
is not the utmost joy.
Shùn taking two daughters,
is not mastering propriety.
Enfeoffing nineteen sons of Huángdì,
is not following the proper way.
Going to the fields and weeping,
is not fulfilling his mandate.
Judging it by human standards,
then it is right.
Measuring it by the law,
then it is not.
The *Lǐ* says:
"There are three hundred rules of etiquette,
and three thousand points of decorum."
The *Shī* says:
"Reverently hold your position,
And side with the upright.
The spirits will listen to you,
And thereby greatly bless you."
4.10 Ritual is,
Governing through argument is the ultimate skill;
it is the foundation of a powerful state;
it is the way to exert authority;
it is the key to achievement and fame.
Kings and dukes follow it,
and thereby unify the world.
If they do not follow it,
they bring about the downfall of their state.
Therefore, strong armor and sharp weapons are not enough to be considered martial prowess;
high walls and deep moats are not enough to be considered secure;
strict orders and numerous punishments are not enough to be considered authoritative.
If one follows the correct way, they will be effective;
if one does not follow the correct way, they will be ineffective.
In the past, the people of Chǔ used the hide of jiāo dragons, rhinoceroses, and sì beasts to make armor,
which was as strong as gold and stone,
winding like giant snakes,
fierce like bees and scorpions,
light, sharp, strong, and swift,
and their soldiers were like a whirlwind.
Yet, their army was defeated at Chuíshā,
Táng Zǐ died,
Zhuāng Qiāo fled,
and Chǔ was divided into three or four parts.
Is it that they did not have strong armor and sharp weapons?
It was because the way they managed them was not the correct one.
They considered the Rǔ and Huái rivers as dangerous barriers,
and the Jiāng and Hàn rivers as moats,
surrounding them with the Fāngchéng wall,
If it were limited by Dèng Lín,
yet the Qin army reached Yān and Yǐng,
and their overthrow was as easy as shaking dry leaves.
Was it truly that they had no strong defenses and dangerous passes?
It was because the way they governed was not the right way.
Zhòu killed Bǐ Gān and imprisoned Jī Zǐ,
instituted the punishment of the "páo luò,"
and engaged in relentless slaughter.
The multitude of subordinates were filled with sorrow and resentment,
and all ceased to expect to live out their lives.
Yet when the Zhou army arrived, orders were not carried out even by those close at hand.
Was it truly that he had no strict orders or numerous punishments?
It was because the way he governed was not the right way.
If one elucidates the Dao and distributes justly,
sincerely loves and employs the people at the right times,
then the response of the lower ranks to the upper ranks will be like echoes.
If some do not follow orders, only
then should they be subjected to punishment. Therefore, punishing one person and the whole world submits,
and the lower ranks do not criticize their superiors,
knowing that the fault lies within themselves.
Thus, punishment gradually disappears, and authority flows freely.
There is no other reason
than that it is due to following the right way.
The *Shī Jīng* says:
"From east, from west,
from south, from north,
there is no one who does not submit."
If it is like this, then those near will sing praises,
Distant people hasten to submit to him.
Even remote and secluded countries all rush to serve him and find peace and happiness.
It is like a red infant returning to its loving mother.
Why is this so?
It is because benevolence and justice are established,
instruction is sincere and love is profound,
therefore their virtue reached to Heaven and Earth,
and their actions were always appropriate.
The *jūnzǐ* is respectful without being difficult,
reverent without being stiff,
poor without being restrained,
rich and noble without being arrogant.
and adaptable without being at a loss.
This is discernment in ritual.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* in ritual,
is reverent and at ease with it.
In his affairs,
he manages them with principle and without error.
In his dealings with people,
he is generous, lenient, and has few grievances, without being obsequious.
In his demeanor,
he is refined in presentation without being affected or precarious.
In his response to changes,
he is swift, responsive, quick, and unencumbered.
In his dealings with the hundred officials and people with skills,
he does not compete with them in ability,
but rather puts their abilities to good use.
Regarding Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things,
he does not go against their nature but carefully regulates their flourishing.
In his treatment of superiors,
he is loyal, obedient, and unwavering.
In his employment of subordinates,
he is fair, comprehensive, and impartial.
In his social interactions,
To categorize and classify things is to have meaning.
In one's village,
be accommodating without creating disorder.
Therefore, when in dire straits, one has a reputation;
when prosperous, one has achievements.
Benevolence and righteousness cover the world without end;
and ritual and music are used to communicate.
The *Shī Jīng* says:
"Rituals and decorum are fully performed,
laughter and cheerful words are fully obtained."
4.11 A ruler distributes benefits according to ritual,
equally and universally without bias.
A subject serves his ruler according to ritual,
with loyalty and obedience that does not falter.
A father is generous and benevolent with ritual,
a son is respectful and shows utmost reverence.
An elder brother is loving and shows friendship,
a younger brother is respectful and not neglectful.
The husband sheds light with distinctions,
the wife is gentle, compliant, and listens.
If one acts without conforming to the proper way,
then one is fearful and self-reproaching.
This is the complete Way.
If one is established in a one-sided way, then there is chaos;
if both are established, then there is order.
May I ask what is required for the simultaneous existence of these abilities?
I say, carefully examine ritual.
In the past, the former kings carefully examined ritual in order to benefit the world,
understanding penetrates Heaven and Earth;
one manages all changes without doubt.
Blood and qi are harmonious;
aspirations and intentions are vast;
practicing righteousness fills Heaven and Earth;
this is the height of benevolence and wisdom.
This is what is called the rites examined by the former kings.
If it is like this,
then the old will be secure,
the young will be cherished,
and friends will trust them,
like a baby returning to its loving mother.
It is said:
With benevolence, punishments are fair; with righteousness, order is established;
with sincere teaching and deep love,
rites and music are interconnected.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"The rites and ceremonies are perfectly measured,

observing human emotions,
understanding the beginning and the end,
knowing gain and loss.
Therefore, he promoted benevolence and righteousness,
detested power and profit,
in order to maintain and nourish [the people].
At this time, the House of Zhou was declining,
the way of the King was cut off,
the feudal lords enforced their own policies,
the strong plundered the weak,
the many tyrannized the few,
the common people had no peace,
there was no standard to guide them,
rites and ceremonies were abandoned and destroyed,
and human relations were disordered.
Therefore, Confucius traveled from east to west,
from south to north,
striving to save the situation.
5.3 The government of a true king is such that
the worthy and capable are promoted without regard to order of precedence,
the unworthy are dismissed without delay,
the chief villains are executed without being reformed,
and the mediocre are transformed without government coercion.
When the ranks have not been determined,
then there are *zhāo* and *mù* (ancestral temple order).
Even if they are the descendants of high ministers and officials,
if their conduct is contrary to rites and ceremonies,
then they are relegated to the common people.
As for those among the people who are inclined to subvert,
observe and test them.
Even if they are the descendants of common people,
if they accumulate learning
and rectify their personal conduct,
If they are capable of propriety and righteousness,
then assign them to the ranks of shì dàfū.
Treat them with respect and wait for them to prove themselves;
if they are settled, then employ them;
if they are unsettled, then discard them.
For rebellious people,
the ruler should take them in and provide for them,
employ those with talent in appropriate tasks,
give official positions and provide them with clothing and food,
and the king will cover all without omission.
Those whose talent and conduct are contrary to the times,
put them to death without pardon,
which is called heavenly punishment.
This is the governance of a true king.
The *Shī* says:
"If a man has no decorum,
what is the point of not dying?"
5.4 A ruler
is the source of the people.
If the source is clear, then the stream will be clear;
if the source is muddy, then the stream will be muddy.
Therefore, one who possesses the altars of soil and grain,
if he cannot love his people,
and yet seeks for the people to be close to him and love him,
it is unattainable.
If the people are not close and do not love him,
and yet seeks that they be employed by him,
and die for him,
It is unattainable.
If the people are not employed by you,
and do not die for you,
and you seek strong soldiers,
and fortified cities,
it is unattainable.
If the soldiers are not strong,
and the cities are not fortified,
and you desire not to be in danger of being weakened, diminished, or destroyed,
it is unattainable.
The conditions for danger, weakening, diminution, and destruction,
all accumulate from this,
and to seek peace and happiness to be heard of,
is this not difficult?
This is a wasted life.
Alas!
A wasted life will perish and be destroyed without delay.
Therefore, if the ruler desires strength, security, peace, and happiness,
nothing is better than examining himself.
If he desires to attach even one commoner,
then nothing is better than implementing benevolent governance.
If he desires to cultivate governance and beautify customs,
then nothing is better than seeking out the right person.
That person,
living in the present age,
but aspiring to the ancient age,
even if all the kings and dukes in the world do not favor it,
but this man alone favors it;
Because the people could not do it,
and this son alone did it.
Perhaps those who did it were exhausted,
and this son still did it,
without the slightest moment of negligence.
Chāi Yān alone understood how the former kings treated people,
and how they lost them.
He knew the security, danger, good, and bad of the state,
as clearly as distinguishing black from white.
Such is the person.
If a ruler wants strength, stability, and peace,
then nothing is better than to act with such a person.
If he is greatly employed,
then the world will become unified,
and the feudal lords will become subjects.
If he is employed in a small way,
then his authority will extend to neighboring countries,
and no one will be able to resist it.
It is like Yīn employing Yī Yǐn,
and Zhōu treating Tài Gōng.
This can be said to be employing him greatly.
Qí employing Guǎn Zhòng,
and Chǔ employing Sūn Shū'áo,
can be said to be employing them in a small way.
Employing him greatly is like that,
and employing him in a small way is like this.
Therefore, it is said:
"Pure and you will be a king,
mixed and you will be a hegemon,
without one and you will perish."
The *Book of Odes* says:
"The four states have no government,
not employing their good men."
Never has there been a case of a state not perishing when it does not employ its good ministers.
One cannot have both proper conduct and
a good reputation simultaneously.
How sorrowful!
If one lives like this,
how can one show oneself to the scholars of the world!"
Thereupon he cut his own throat and died.
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"Advancing or retreating, all is difficulty."
10.25 Formerly, Tài Gōng Wàng 太公望 and Zhōu Gōng Dàn 周公旦 received their fiefs and had an audience.
Tài Gōng 太公 asked Zhōu Gōng 周公 how he would govern Lǔ 魯.
Zhōu Gōng 周公 said:
"Respect the honorable and be affectionate to relatives."
Tài Gōng 太公 said:
"Lǔ 魯 will become weak from this."
Zhōu Gōng 周公 asked Tài Gōng 太公, saying:
"How will you govern Qí 齊?"
Tài Gōng 太公 said:
"Promote the worthy and reward merit."
Zhōu Gōng 周公 said:
"In later generations, there will surely be a ruler who is robbed and killed."
After this, Qí 齊 grew larger day by day,
until it became a hegemon.
After twenty-four generations, the Tián 田 clan replaced the ruling house.
Lǔ 魯 was diminished day by day,
and was extinguished after thirty-four generations.
Judging from this,
sages are able to understand the subtle.
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"Only this sage,
looks ahead hundreds of *lǐ*."
There has never been such a case.
5.5 Zào Fù,
was the best chariot driver in the world,
but without chariots and horses, there would be no way to see his ability.
Yì,
was the best archer in the world,
but without bows and arrows, there would be no way to see his skill.
Those great Confucian scholars
are the ones who harmonize the entire world;
without a territory of a hundred *lǐ*, there would be no way to see their accomplishments.
If carriages are sturdy and horses are well-chosen, but they cannot travel a thousand *lǐ*,
then it is not Zào Fù.
If bows are well-tuned and arrows are straight, but they cannot shoot far and hit subtle targets,
then it is not Yì.
If, using a territory of a hundred *lǐ*, one cannot harmonize the entire world and control the four barbarian tribes,
then it is not a great Confucian scholar.
Those great Confucian scholars,
even if they live in seclusion in poor alleys and humble dwellings,
without a piece of land to stand on,
kings and dukes cannot compete with them for fame.
If employed in a territory of a hundred *lǐ*,
even a kingdom of a thousand *lǐ* cannot compete with them for victory.
To whip and scourge violent states,
to unify the entire world,
and no one can overthrow it,
this is the accomplishment of a great Confucian scholar. Their words are consistent,
His conduct is according to ritual,
his actions are without regret,
his adherence to restraint and response to change are always appropriate,
he moves with the times,
he rises and falls with the world,
through a thousand actions and myriad changes,
his way is one,
this is the standard of a great Ru.
Therefore, there are vulgar people,
there are vulgar Ru,
there are refined Ru,
there are great Ru.
His ears do not hear learning,
his conduct lacks proper righteousness,
he is completely absorbed in making wealth and profit his priority,
this is a vulgar person.
He wears long gowns and wide belts,
superficially imitates the former kings but is sufficient to throw the world into chaos,
his techniques are flawed and his learning is mixed,
his actions do not know to model themselves after the later kings in order to unify the institutions,
he does not know to elevate ritual and righteousness but slights the *Classic of Poetry* and *Classic of Documents*,
his (incorrectly adorned) attire, cap, speech, and conduct are already identical to worldly customs,
yet he does not know their evil.
His speech and discussions are already no different from those of the old Mò (Mozi),
yet he does not know to differentiate.
This is a vulgar Ru.
He models himself after the former kings,
unifying the institutions,
Speech and action have great principles;
but clear judgment cannot encompass where the law and teachings do not reach,
where hearing and seeing have not yet arrived.
To know when one knows,
to not know when one does not know,
not deceiving oneself internally,
not deceiving others externally,
with this, one respects the worthy and reveres the law,
and dares not be lazy or arrogant.
This is a *yǎ rú* (雅儒) scholar.
Taking the former kings as a model, relying on propriety and righteousness,
using the shallow to grasp the broad,
using one action to regulate myriad affairs.
If there is anything resembling benevolence and righteousness,
then even birds and beasts seem to distinguish black from white.
Strange objects and unusual occurrences,
which have never been heard or seen,
should they suddenly arise in one region,
then one can bring the overall categories to respond to them,
without doubt.
Drawing upon the law and measuring by it,
it fits perfectly, like matching tallies.
This is a *dà rú* (大儒) scholar.
Therefore, if a ruler employs common people,
then a state of ten thousand chariots will perish.
If he employs common scholars,
then a state of ten thousand chariots will survive.
If he employs *yǎ rú* (雅儒) scholars,
Then a state of a thousand *lǐ* will be secure.
Employ great scholars,
then a territory of a hundred *lǐ* will last long,
and in three years,
the world will be unified,
and the feudal lords will become subjects.
Employ a state with ten thousand chariots, then actions will be determined
within a single morning.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Although Zhou is an old state,
its mandate is renewed."
King Wen may indeed be called a great scholar.
5.6 King Chéng of Chǔ was reading a book in the palace,
and Lún Biǎn was below.
He rose and asked:
"May I inquire what book Your Majesty is reading?"
King Chéng said:
"The books of the former sages."
Lún Biǎn said:
"These are truly the dregs of the former sage kings.
They are not the best."
King Chéng said:
"How do you say that?"
Lún Biǎn said:
"Let me explain with my wheel-making.
To make a circle with a compass and
a square with a ruler,
This is what can be passed on to one's descendants.
As for joining three pieces of wood into one,
responding with the heart,
moving the body,
these are things that cannot be obtained and transmitted.
Then all that is transmitted is mere dregs."
Therefore, the laws of Táng Yú can be obtained and examined.
But their understanding of the human heart is unattainable.
The *Shī* says:
"What Heaven loads on us,
has neither sound nor smell."
Who can attain it?
5.7 Kǒngzǐ learned to play the qín from Shī Xiāngzǐ, but did not advance.
Shī Xiāngzǐ said:
"Master, you may advance now."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Qiū has already grasped the melody,
but has not yet grasped the technique."
After a while,
Shī Xiāngzǐ said:
"Master, you may advance now."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Qiū has already grasped the technique,
but has not yet grasped the meaning."
After a while,
Shī Xiāngzǐ again said:
"Master, you may advance now."
Kǒngzǐ said:
has already found the man,
but has not yet found his kind."
After a while,
he said:
"Gazing far away,
vast and expansive, dignified and respectful,
he must have created this music.
Pondering in silence,
feeling sorrowful and disappointed,
to rule the world,
and to have the lords pay court,
it must be Wén Wáng!"
Shī Xiāngzi stepped aside from his mat and bowed twice, saying:
"Excellent!
I believed it was the melody of Wén Wáng."
Therefore, Confucius, holding the melody of Wén Wáng,
knew the person of Wén Wáng.
Shī Xiāngzi said:
"May I ask how you know it is the melody of Wén Wáng?"
Confucius said:
"Indeed.
The benevolent like grandeur,
the harmonious like embellishment,
the wise like plucking (stringed instruments),
and those with a sincere and diligent mind like elegance.
That is how I know it is the melody of Wén Wáng."
The *Commentary* says:
"Those who hear the end and understand the beginning
He was a sage.
5.8 Zhòu, as ruler,
exhausted the people's strength,
and cruel and unjust decrees
were imposed on the common people;
ruthless and sorrowful evils
were inflicted upon high officials.
The lower ranks did not trust him,
and the people were filled with resentment and hatred.
Therefore, the world rebelled and desired to be vassals of Wén Wáng.
Zhòu brought it upon himself.
To be esteemed as the Son of Heaven,
and possess the wealth of the world,
yet when the Zhōu army arrived, his orders were not carried out by those at his side—
how sad!
At that time,
even if he sought to be a commoner,
it would not have been possible.
The *Shī* says:
"The Heavenly seat was fitting for Yīn,
but it did not extend to all four quarters."
5.9 Although the five colors are bright,
they sometimes fade.
Even a tree with abundant branches
sometimes loses its leaves.
Things have periods of flourishing and decline,
and cannot remain as they are.
Therefore, the way of the Three Kings,
reaches a full cycle and then begins anew.
When exhausted, it returns to its roots.
It is not merely concerned with change,
but rather with stopping evil and supporting the weak,
removing falsehood and eliminating what is wrong,
harmonizing *yīn* and *yáng*,
and conforming to the suitability of all things.
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"Strive, strive, our King,
be the guiding principle for the four quarters."
5.10 Ritual is patterned after the structure of Heaven and Earth,
and establishes proper regulations based on human feelings. Teachers are those who correct ritual.
Without ritual,
how can one rectify oneself?
Without teachers,
how can one know that ritual is correct?
When ritual is naturally followed,
it is because feelings are at ease within ritual.
When one speaks as the teacher speaks,
it is because one's knowledge resembles that of the teacher.
When feelings are at ease with ritual,
and knowledge resembles that of the teacher,
then this is the way of the noble person (*jūnzǐ*).
When words accord with ethical relationships (*lún*),
and actions accord with principle (*lǐ*),
the world will be in harmony.
The *Shī* says:
"Without knowledge or awareness,
they follow the model of Emperor Shùn."
5.11 If superiors do not know to follow filial piety,
then the people will not know to return to their roots.
If the ruler does not know to respect elders,
then the people will not know to value their relatives.
If the *dì* sacrifice is not reverent,
and offerings to mountains and rivers are not timely,
then the people will have nothing to fear.
Punishing without teaching
means the people will not understand encouragement.
Therefore, if the *jūnzǐ* cultivates himself and extends to filial piety,
then the people will not turn their backs.
When respect and filial piety reach those below,
then the people will know kindness and love.
When likes and dislikes are made clear to the common people,
then those below will respond to their superiors like an echo.
This is the essential method
for concurrently governing the world,
stabilizing the country,
and controlling the myriad people, which enlightened kings and sage rulers cannot afford to abandon even for a moment.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"The trustworthiness of King Chéng,
is the standard for the land below.
Forever speaking of filial thoughts,
filial thoughts are the model."
5.12 In the time of King Chéng,
three sprouts grew through a mulberry tree and sprouted,
Being the same single ear of grain,
large numbers filled a cart,
long stalks filled a chest,
King Chéng asked the Duke of Zhōu,
"What are these things?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"The Sān Miáo all grew the same single ear of grain,
I suspect the world is probably unified."
Almost three years later,
successively, there were people from the Yuè Cháng tribe, coming via nine translations,
presenting a white pheasant to the Duke of Zhōu:
"The roads are distant and long,
the mountains and rivers are secluded and deep.
Fearing that our messengers would not reach you,
therefore, we have come via multiple translations."
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"What have I been given?"
The translator said:
"We received the command from the yellow-haired elders of our country saying:
'It has been a long time since the heavens sent quick winds and heavy rains,
and the sea has not had overflowing waves,
it has been three years now.
I suspect that China probably has a sage?
Why not go and pay homage to him?'
Therefore, we have come."
The Duke of Zhōu then respectfully sought out the reason for their coming.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"For ten thousand years,
bù xiá yǒu zuǒ." (Will) not have assistance from afar."
5.13 Climbing high and overlooking the deep,
the pleasure of seeing far,
terraces and pavilions are not as good as hills and mountains in terms of height.
Viewing widely on a plain,
the pleasure of broad observation,
ponds and pools are not as good as rivers and lakes in terms of breadth.
Toiling the mind with bitter thought,
indulging desires to the utmost,
wasting wealth and hurting feelings,
ruining reputation and damaging lifespan.
How sad and lamentable!
A ruler depleted (by this) turns against this way and worries the common people.
The *Shī* says:
"Shàngdì bǎn bǎn,
xià mín zú dàn." ("God is unjust, the people are utterly weary.")
5.14 *Rúzhě*, (are) *rú* (scholars).
The meaning of *rú* is "nothing,"
(it represents) an unchanging method.
Through a thousand undertakings and ten thousand changes,
its Dao is inexhaustible;
this is the Six Classics.
As for the righteousness between ruler and subject,
the affection between father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
the order between friends,
these are what the *rúzhě* cautiously guard,
diligently striving for improvement without ceasing.
Even though they live in humble alleys and cramped rooms,
their inner selves are not left unfulfilled,
and their outer appearances are not left uncovered.
Though they possess not even enough land to place an awl,
their keen insight is sufficient to govern the world,
and their great actions would place them above others.
Then they are the stuff of kings and dukes.
If employed in a lesser capacity while in office,
then they are ministers of the state.
Even if they dwell in caves and live in holes, kings and nobles cannot compete with them for fame.
Why?
Because the transformative power of benevolence and righteousness resides within them.
If a ruler were to heed their words
and trust their actions,
then the laws of Táng Yú could be seen,
and songs of praise could be heard.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"The people of old had a saying:
Consult the grass-cutters and fuel-gatherers."
This is to show the breadth of seeking counsel.
5.15 The *Zhuàn* (Commentary) says:
"The Son of Heaven dwells beneath broad mansions,
within curtains and screens,
upon rugs of felt,
wearing slippers,
his gaze not extending beyond the threshold.
Yet he vaguely knows the world,
because of his virtuous advisors."
Therefore, seeing alone is not as clear as seeing with the crowd;
listening alone is not as sharp as listening with the crowd.
Thinking alone is not as effective as thinking with the crowd.
Therefore, enlightened rulers cause virtuous ministers to
converge and advance together,
in order to achieve impartiality and attract hidden scholars.
The *Shi Jing* (Classic of Poetry) says:
"The people of old had a saying:
consult the grass cutters and fuel gatherers."
This is what it means.
5.16 Heaven established its height,
and the sun and moon achieved brightness.
Earth established its thickness,
and mountains and hills achieved fame.
The sovereign established his Dao,
and all affairs obtained order.
Since the decline and decay of the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
the Kingly Way was abandoned and did not rise,
rites and righteousness were cut off and not continued.
During the time of Qín 秦,
they rejected rites and righteousness,
discarded the *Shi* 詩 (Poetry) and *Shū* 書 (Documents),
disregarded antiquity,
greatly destroyed the way of the sages,
focused solely on expedience and falsehood,
took greed for profit as custom,
and made competitive hunting a form of education,
And the world was greatly disordered.
Thereupon, weapons were made and fires started;
people were exposed and lived outdoors.
The people considered plundering, encroaching, obstructing, and seizing from each other as commonplace habits.
They were far removed from the glorious days of the sage kings.
They had never seen the way of benevolence and righteousness
and were not influenced by the winds of ritual and music.
Therefore, they were obstinate and unruly, lacking in propriety,
while reverence and respect decreased day by day.
They used intimidation and force to control each other.
They acted recklessly as sycophants,
not avoiding calamity and suffering.
This is why they were difficult to govern.
People have six emotions.
The eyes desire to see beautiful colors,
the ears desire to hear palace music,
the nose desires to smell fragrant scents,
the mouth desires to savor delicious flavors,
and the body and limbs desire to be comfortable and at ease.
Clothing should be adorned with embroidery and be light and warm.
These six things
are the six emotions of the people.
Lose them, and there is chaos;
follow them, and there is harmony.
Therefore, when sage kings taught their people,
they invariably accommodated their emotions but regulated them with ritual;
they invariably followed their desires but controlled them with righteousness.
Righteousness was simple and comprehensive,
Rites are easy and lawful,
not far removed from human feelings,
therefore the people are quick to follow orders.
Kǒngzǐ knew that the Way was easy to practice, saying:
"The *Book of Poetry* says:
'Guiding the people is very easy.'
These are not empty words."
5.17 The nature of the silkworm cocoon is to be silk,
but if it does not get the labor of women to boil it in hot water,
and draw out its threads in order,
it will not become silk.
The nature of an egg is to be a chick,
but if it does not get a good hen to cover, incubate, and nurture it,
accumulating days and months,
it will not become a chick.
Human nature is good,
but if it does not get an enlightened king and sage ruler to support and guide it,
and instill it with the Way,
it will not become a *jūnzǐ*.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Heaven gives birth to the multitudes,
their mandate is not constant,
none do not have a beginning,
but few are able to have an end."
It means that only an enlightened king and sage ruler can make it so.
5.18 One whose wisdom is like a spring,
and whose conduct can be a model for others,
A teacher of men.
One whose wisdom can be sharpened,
and whose actions can serve as assistance,
is a friend of men.
One who adheres to the law and guards his duty,
and dares not do wrong,
is an officer of men.
One who seeks immediate gratification,
and echoes every command with a double "yes,"
is a servant of men.
Therefore, a superior ruler takes teachers as his assistants,
a middling ruler takes friends as his assistants,
an inferior ruler takes officers as his assistants,
and a ruler heading for destruction takes servants as his assistants.
A saying goes:
"In a deep pool, the fish are large;
under an enlightened ruler, the ministers are wise."
Observing each other and uniting in purpose
must come from within.
Therefore, those of similar brightness see each other;
those of similar sound hear each other;
those of similar aspiration follow each other.
None but the wise can employ the wise.
Therefore, those who assist on the left and right,
those who are entrusted and employed,
hold the key to survival or ruin,
and the essentials of gain or loss.
Can one be without caution?
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
"If you do not understand your virtue,
You will have no support or assistance.
If you do not understand your virtue,
You will have no attendants or ministers."
5.19 In the past, Yǔ took the Xia as king,
and Jié caused the Xia to perish.
Tāng took the Yin as king,
and Zhòu caused the Yin to perish.
Therefore, there is no perpetually secure state,
nor a people that should only be governed.
If they gain the worthy, they prosper;
if they have the unworthy, they perish.
From ancient times until now,
there has never been an exception to this.
A clear mirror is for reflecting one's form;
the past is for understanding the present.
To know why the past was endangered and perished,
but not follow what enabled it to survive,
is no different from walking backward and trying to catch up with those ahead.
A common saying goes:
"If you don't know how to be an official,
look at what has already been accomplished."
Or it is said:
"If the carriage in front overturns and the carriage behind does not take warning,
then the carriage behind will also overturn."
Therefore, what caused the Xia to perish, the Yin did;
what caused the Yin to perish, the Zhōu did.
Therefore, Yīn can be a mirror for Xià,
and Zhōu can be a mirror for Yīn.
The *Shī* [Classic of Poetry] says:
"The Yīn mirror is not far off;
it lies in the era of the Xià sovereign."
The *Zhuàn* [Commentary] says:
Overbearing and arrogant rulers have few loyal subjects, and those who give only lip service have little trustworthiness.
Therefore, a handful-sized tree has no branches that can be embraced, and a glorious and ample body of water has no fish that can swallow boats.
Shallow roots result in short branches and leaves, and when the root is severed, the branches and leaves wither.
The *Shī* [Classic of Poetry] says:
"When the branches and leaves are not yet harmed,
the root has already been disturbed."
Calamity and fortune come from oneself.
When a body of water is deep and wide,
dragons and fish are born there.
When mountains and forests are lush and flourishing,
birds and beasts return to them.
When ritual propriety and righteousness are cultivated and clarified,
gentlemen cherish them.
Therefore, when ritual propriety extends to oneself, conduct is cultivated;
when ritual propriety extends to the state, governance is enlightened.
If one can use ritual propriety to support oneself,
then noble reputation will naturally be proclaimed,
the world will submit to them,
orders will be carried out and prohibitions will be heeded,
and the affairs of a king will be complete.
When commands are carried out and prohibitions are enforced,
then the affairs of a true king are completed.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"He possessed conscious virtue and conduct,
and the four states submitted to him."
This is what it means.
5.22 Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the art of discourse,
establish it with reverence and solemnity,
conduct it with uprightness and sincerity,
maintain it with firmness and strength,
illustrate it with analogies,
clarify it by distinctions,
and conclude it with joy and fragrance,
treasure it, value it,
esteem it, and regard it as divine.
If you do so, then your words will invariably be effective.
This is what it means to be able to value what is valuable.
As for discourses that are without order,
actions that are unprincipled,
and words that are unsubstantiated,
the *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) is cautious of them."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Do not lightly utter words,
do not say it is merely a casual remark." 5.23 When the common people
internally do not lack food
and externally are not troubled by cold,
Then they can be taught to govern with propriety and righteousness.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"We present the steamed offerings to our ancestors,
So that all rites are fulfilled."
