but he quickly relied on Jiù Fàn,
Zhào Cuī, and Jiè Zǐtuī, and eventually became a ruler.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè (Yuè Wáng Gōujiàn) was besieged at Kuàijī,
but he quickly relied on Fàn Lǐ and Grandee Zhǒng, and achieved hegemony in the southern states.
Duke Huán of Qí (Qí Huán Gōng) was troubled at Chángsháo,
but he quickly relied on Guǎn Zhòng, Níng Qī, and Xí Péng, and rectified the world.
All these are examples of those who, in distress, knew to quickly rely on worthy individuals.
As for those who are in distress and do not know to quickly rely on worthy individuals and yet do not perish,
there has never been such a case.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"When people are gone,
the state is utterly exhausted."
This refers to the absence of good people.
6.14 Mencius spoke to King Xuān of Qí (Qí Xuān Wáng) but was not heeded.
Chúnyú Kūn was in attendance.
Mencius said,
"Today I spoke to your ruler,
but your ruler did not heed me.
Could it be that he does not yet know what is good as good?"
Chúnyú Kūn said,
"Master, you truly lack goodness.
In the past, Hù Bā played the zither and the submerged fish came out to listen,
Bó Yá played the qín, and the six horses raised their heads to listen to the music.
Fish and horses even know good when they see it,
how much more so should a ruler of men?"
Mèng Zǐ said:
"When thunder and lightning arise,
breaking bamboo and snapping trees,
shaking and startling the world,
they still cannot suddenly enable a deaf person to hear.
The brightness of the sun and moon,
shines universally on the world,
yet cannot suddenly enable a blind person to see.
Your ruler is like this."
Chún Yú Kūn said:
"That is not so.
In the past, Yī Fēng was granted the title of Shēng Gāo Shāng;
the people of Qí loved to sing.
The wife of Qǐ Liáng cried mournfully,
and people praised her.
There is no sound so small that it cannot be heard,
no action so hidden that it does not take shape.
If you, Master, are truly virtuous,
how is it that you resided in Lǔ and the state of Lǔ was diminished?
Why is this?"
Mèng Zǐ said:
"If the virtuous are not employed,
what does diminution matter?
Fish that can swallow boats do not live in shallow swamps,
men of great capacity do not live in a corrupt world.
Now, when the artemisia fades in the winter solstice,
it is also my time.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Neither I precede,
nor I follow."
Is it not like one who encounters a degenerate age?"
6.15 Confucius said:
"One with whom you can speak all day without tiring,
is surely one who learns.
Their physical body is not worth looking at,
their courage and strength are not worth fearing,
their clan name is not worth mentioning,
their ancestors are not worth talking about,
yet they can be heard in all directions
and be known among the lords,
is surely one who learns."
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Not exceeding, not forgetting,
following the old rules."
This is what learning is about.
6.16 Confucius said:
"If one does not know destiny,
there is no way to be a gentleman (*jūnzǐ*)."
It means that what Heaven creates,
all have hearts of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, obedience, and goodness.
If one does not know why Heaven ordains life,
then one does not have hearts of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, obedience, and goodness.
Those who lack the hearts of rén, yì, lǐ, zhì, shùn, and shàn
are called petty people (xiǎorén).
Therefore, it is said:
"Not knowing fate,
one cannot be a junzi."
The *Xiaoya* (Lesser Odes) says:
"Heaven protects and establishes you;
Indeed, it is most secure."
This speaks of how Heaven's rén, yì, lǐ, and zhì
secure people in a most steadfast way.
The *Daya* (Greater Odes) says:
"Heaven gives birth to the multitude of people;
There are things and there are rules.
The people grasp their constant nature;
They love this beautiful virtue."
This speaks of how the people grasp virtue in order to follow Heaven.
If one does not know how to follow Heaven,
how can one be a junzi?
6.17 A king must establish *mù*,
two men per region,
to have them observe from afar and oversee the multitude.
If among the people of distant regions there are those who are hungry and cold but cannot obtain clothing and food,
or those who have lawsuits but whose grievances are not redressed,
or those who have lost the worthy and do not promote them,
they enter and report to the Son of Heaven (tiānzǐ).
When the Son of Heaven is at his ruler's court,
he bows and advances them,
saying:
"Alas,"
"is it possible that there are shortcomings in my governance and teachings?
Why is it that there are those who suffer from hunger and cold and lack clothing and food,
those who have lawsuits but their grievances are not redressed,
and those who are talented but not promoted?"
Thereupon, the ruler would withdraw and consult with his high officials.
The people of distant lands, hearing of this,
would all say,
"Truly, this is a Son of Heaven!
He considers the secluded place where I live,
and sees that I am close to him;
he considers the obscurity in which I live,
and sees that I am intelligent.
Can he be deceived?"
Therefore, the ruler opens
his four eyes
and uses his four ears for information.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says,
"When the state is in trouble,
Zhòng Shānfǔ clarifies it."
This is what it means.
6.18 King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng, bare-chested,
held a cattail banner in his left hand
and grasped a luan-decorated knife in his right hand,
and went forward to speak to King Zhuāng,
saying,
"I, a man of little virtue, have subjects on the borders
who offended against your grand proclamation,
causing the ruler of a great nation to be angered,
and to endure the humiliation of coming this far."
Zhuāng Wáng 莊王 said,
"A gentleman does not command his subjects,
but speaks through negotiations.
It is for this reason that I, a man of little virtue, was able to see your jade-like face,
and to arrive in this humble place."
Zhuāng Wáng 莊王 accepted the token of submission,
and with a gesture to his attendants, the Chǔ 楚 army retreated seven *lǐ* 里.
General Zǐ Zhòng 子重 advanced to remonstrate, saying,
"The distance between Nányǐng 南郢 and Zhèng 鄭
is several thousand *lǐ* 里.
Several officers have died,
and hundreds of servants have perished.
Now, having conquered it, we do not possess it;
is this not a loss of the strength of our people and ministers?"
Zhuāng Wáng 莊王 said,
"I have heard that in ancient times, the shaft did not penetrate,
and the leather did not decay,
if they did not originate from all four corners [of the realm].
This is how a gentleman values propriety and devalues wealth;
he desires the people,
not the land.
To persist when one is told to yield is inauspicious.
It is not auspicious.
If I were to establish myself in the world with something inauspicious,
"Calamity will befall me personally.
What advantage is there to be gained?"
Soon after,
the rescuers of Zhèng 鄭 from Jìn 晉 arrived,
and said,
"We request battle."
King Zhuāng 莊 of Chǔ 楚 granted it.
General Zǐ Zhòng 子重 remonstrated, saying,
"Jìn 晉 is
a powerful state.
Their route is short, and their soldiers are keen.
The Chǔ 楚 army has just been demobilized.
Your Majesty, you must not grant it."
King Zhuāng 莊 said,
"That will not do.
If I avoid the strong
and only intimidate the weak,
then I, the lonely one, will have no way to establish myself in the world."
Thereupon, he returned his army to meet the Jìn 晉 invaders.
King Zhuāng 莊 took up the drumstick and beat the drum.
The Jìn 晉 army was utterly defeated.
The soldiers fled, fighting for boats, and those killed could be picked up by the handful.
King Zhuāng 莊 said,
"Alas!
Our two rulers are not on good terms,
but what crime have the common people committed!"
He then withdrew the Chǔ 楚 army to allow the Jìn 晉 invaders to rest.
The *Book of Odes* says,
"The gentle he does not devour,
the strong he does not reject."
6.19 The *jūnzǐ* reveres the virtues of others,
and praises the beauty of others;
this is not flattery against principle.
Speaking correctly and acting straight,
pointing out the faults of others,
this is not destructive criticism.
Being yielding, gentle, compliant and obedient;
and being firm, strong, fierce, and resolute;
harmonizing with things,
moral principles are not violated.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"The gentle he does not devour,
the strong he does not reject,
he does not insult the lonely widows and widowers,
he does not fear the powerful and aggressive."
6.20 Wèi Líng Gōng took a nap during the day and awoke,
his spirit and vigor were even more diminished,
so he sent someone to summon the brave warrior Gōngsūn Yuān with haste.
On the way, the messenger encountered the traveler Bǔ Shāng.
Bǔ Shāng said,
"Why do you rush so quickly?"
The messenger replied,
"The Duke took a nap during the day and awoke,
and has sent me to summon the brave warrior Gōngsūn Yuān."
Zǐxià said,
"Is Yuān unimportant?
"How about someone whose courage seems rash?"
The charioteer said,
"Acceptable."
Zǐ Xià said,
"Turn back and take me."
Upon arrival,
the ruler said,
"I sent you to summon a brave warrior.
Why did you summon a Confucian scholar?"
The messenger said,
"The traveler said,
'Someone slightly rash,
is someone whose courage seems rash acceptable?'
I said,
'Acceptable.'
So I brought him along."
The ruler said,
"Okay,
invite the gentleman up.
Quickly, summon Gōngsūn Yuān."
Upon his arrival,
he entered the gate, brandishing his sword and shouting loudly,
saying,
"Shāng, come down!
I'm here to keep your head on your shoulders."
Zǐ Xià turned and scolded him,
saying,
"Hey!
The inner sword.
I will speak to you about courage."
Thereupon the lord ordered the inner sword to be brought up.
Zǐxià 子夏 said:
"Come!
I once accompanied you, following the lord westward to meet Zhào Jiǎnzi 趙簡子.
Jiǎnzi 簡子 met our lord with disheveled hair and holding a spear.
I, from behind the thirteenth rank,
hastened forward and said:
'When feudal lords meet,
it is not appropriate not to wear court robes.
If court robes are not worn,
the herald Bǔ Shāng 卜商 will stain your robes with the blood from his neck.'
Causing him to change into court robes to meet our lord,
was that you or me?"
Yuān 悁 said:
"It was you."
Zǐxià 子夏 said:
"Your courage is not as great as mine in this one instance.
Furthermore, accompanying you, following the lord eastward to Ā 阿,
we encountered the lord of Qí 齊 sitting on multiple mats.
Our lord was sitting on a single mat.
I, from behind the thirteenth rank,
hastened forward and said:
'According to ritual,
when feudal lords meet,
it is not appropriate to disrespect each other with commonness.'
The one who took away one of his mats,
"Was it you or I?"
Yuān said:
"It was you."
Zǐxià said:
"Your bravery is not as great as mine in two respects.
Another time, you and I were following the ruler in the park,
when two bandits, shoulder to shoulder, pursued our ruler.
Drawing my spear, I struck downwards and drove them back.
Was it you or I?"
Yuān said:
"It was you."
Zǐxià said:
"Your bravery is not as great as mine in three respects.
What is valued in being a shì (gentleman-scholar)
is to oversee the myriad chariots above,
and below, not dare to be arrogant towards commoners.
Outwardly, establishing integrity and dignity so that enemies do not invade or disturb;
inwardly, prohibiting brutality and harm so that the ruler is not in danger.
This is what a shì excels at, and what a jūnzǐ (superior man) values and pursues.
As for using strengths to cover up weaknesses,
using the many to oppress the few,
trampling on innocent people,
and establishing a reputation for power in the lanes and alleys,
this is the greatest poison of a shì and what a jūnzǐ detests,
and what the masses condemn and eradicate.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
'If a man has no decorum,
why does he not die?'
How should one discuss courage before a ruler!"
Thereupon, Duke Líng stepped away from his mat, lowered his hand, and said,
"Although I am not intelligent,
I ask to follow your courage, Master."
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Do not insult the lonely and widowed,
Do not fear the strong and violent."
This describes Master Bǔ.
6.21 Kǒngzǐ was traveling,
Jiǎn Zǐ was about to kill Yáng Hǔ,
Kǒngzǐ resembled him,
and they surrounded Kǒngzǐ's lodging with armored soldiers.
Zǐ Lù was angry,
brandished his halberd, and was about to descend.
Kǒngzǐ stopped him and said:
"Yóu!
How little humanity and righteousness you possess!
That the *Book of Poetry* and *Book of Documents* are not practiced,
and that rituals and music are not explained,
this is my fault.
If I am not Yáng Hǔ, but they mistake me for Yáng Hǔ,
then it is not my fault.
It is fate! I
will sing and you harmonize."
Zǐ Lù sang,
Kǒngzǐ harmonized,
and after three stanzas, the siege was lifted.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Lái yóu lái gē."
This is to display the harmony and wúwéi of flourishing virtue.
6.22 The *Shī* says:
"Kǎitì junzi,
mín zhī fùmǔ."
What is it like for a jūnzi to be the parents of the people?
He said:
A jūnzi
is respectful in appearance but unconstrained in action,
frugal in personal life but generous in giving,
therefore the unworthy cannot keep up with him.
He cultivates everything fully in himself
but only aims for an outline in others,
therefore one can devote oneself entirely to serving him.
He deeply loves without seizing,
and generously gives without boasting.
When he sees good in others,
he is delighted and rejoices;
when he sees evil in others,
he is cautiously covering it up;
and he encompasses their faults.
He bestows clothing with the finest,
and bestows food in abundance.
Laws are easy to follow below,
and affairs are few and easy to handle.
Therefore, he is impartial and acts as the parents of the people.
He builds cities for them to live in,
To separate fields and support them,
and establish schools to teach them,
enables people to know and revere their parents.
Because they revere their parents, the father wears the mourning garments of *zhǎncuī* for three years;
in the case of the ruler, they also wear the *zhǎncuī* for three years, this is what it means to regard the common people as parents.
6.23 To serve a strong and tyrannical country is difficult,
but to make a strong and tyrannical country serve me is easy.
If we serve them with goods and treasures,
then the treasures will be depleted and the relationship will not be secure.
If we make agreements and oaths,
then the agreements will be made, but the betrayal will not be far off.
If we cede the strength of the state to appease them,
then the cession will be made, but their desires will not be satisfied.
The more we serve them obsequiously,
the more severely they will encroach upon us,
and it will surely end with the exhaustion of our treasures and the complete takeover of our state.
Even if we had Yáo on the left and Shùn on the right,
there has never been anyone who could avoid this fate by this method.
Therefore, if one does not possess the Dao of a sage,
and relies solely on cleverness and agility to humbly request, plead, fear, and serve them,
then it is insufficient to maintain the state and secure one's own life.
Therefore, a wise ruler does not act in such a way.
He must cultivate ritual propriety to regulate the court,
rectify laws to regulate the officials,
and equalize governance to regulate the people below.
Then ritual propriety and measured conduct will be regulated in the court,
laws and standards will be rectified among the officials,
Loyalty, trustworthiness, love, and benefit should be equally distributed to those below.
One should not commit a single unjust act,
nor kill a single innocent person,
even if it means gaining the entire world.
Therefore, those nearby will compete to be close, and those far away will desire to come.
When superiors and inferiors are of one mind,
and the three armies exert their strength together,
a reputation will be enough to influence them,
and powerful prestige will be enough to unify them.
Then, with hands clasped and directions given,
even the most violent and tyrannical states will not fail to be submissive, like infants returning to their loving mother.
Why is this?
Because benevolence is embodied and righteousness is established,
and because instruction is sincere and love is profound.
Therefore, the *Book of Poetry* says:
"The king's plans are truly effective,
and the lands of Xú are already coming."
6.24 One shout from a brave warrior will cause all three armies to retreat.
This is the sincerity of a soldier.
In the past, Xióng Qú of Chǔ was walking at night,
and he saw a sleeping stone and thought it was a crouching tiger.
He drew his bow and shot it,
burying the arrowhead and feather shaft in the stone.
When he looked down,
he realized it was a stone,
and the stone opened up because of it.
How much more so with people?
Now, if one initiates but there is no harmony,
and one moves but there is no achievement,
then there must be something incomplete in the heart.
Now, if one wants to rectify the world without leaving one's mat,
then one must seek it within oneself.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If one's person is upright..."
he will be followed even without orders;
if his person is not upright,
he will not be obeyed even with orders."
The reason why the former kings could simply bow and gesture, and the four seas would come as guests,
was because their sincere virtue was supreme,
and it manifested outwardly in their countenance.
The *Shī* 詩 (Book of Odes) says:
"The king's plans were truly effective,
and the Xú 徐 region then came."
6.25 In the past, when Zhào Jiǎnzi 趙簡子 died but had not yet been buried,
the city of Zhōngmóu 中牟 rebelled.
Five days after the burial,
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 raised an army and attacked it.
Before the siege was complete,
ten *zhàng* 丈 (approx. 100 feet) of the city wall collapsed on its own.
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 struck the gong and withdrew the troops.
A military officer advised,
"Your Lordship is punishing Zhōngmóu 中牟 for its crime, and the city wall collapses on its own;
this is Heaven assisting you!
Why does Your Lordship withdraw?"
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 said,
"I heard Shū Xiàng 叔向 say:
"A junzi
(君子) does not take advantage of others' profit, nor does he corner others in danger."
Wait until the city is fortified before attacking it.
Zhōngmóu (中牟) heard of his righteousness and requested to surrender,
saying,
"Excellent!
This is what Xiāngzǐ (襄子) is all about."
The *Shī* (詩, Book of Poetry) says:
"The king's plans are truly substantial,
the Xú (徐) region has already come to submit."
6.26 There are three methods of power (wēi 威).
There is the power of moral virtue,
the power of violent scrutiny, and
the power of wild arrogance.
These three types of power must be carefully examined.
What is the power of moral virtue?
It is said:
When ritual and music are cultivated,
divisions of righteousness are clear,
actions are timely,
and love and benefit are according to standards,
then
the people will value him like an emperor,
be intimate with him like parents,
and fear him like deities.
Therefore, rewards are not needed yet the people are encouraged,
punishments are not applied yet power is exerted.
This is the power of moral virtue.
What is meant by the "might of tyrannical scrutiny" (bào chá zhī wēi)?
It means:
Ritual and music (lǐ yuè) are not cultivated.
Distinctions in righteousness (fēn yì) are not made clear.
Actions (jǔ cuò) are not taken at the proper time.
Affection and profit (ài lì) are not used to guide punishment (xíng).
Yet the prohibitions are unusually severe (bào).
Punishments for disobedience are excessive and thorough (fán shěn).
Penalties are heavy and reliable.
Executions are fierce and certain.
They fall swiftly, like a thunderbolt.
Like a wall collapsing.
The people, when threatened, show respect.
When relaxed, they become arrogant towards their superiors.
When detained, they gather together.
When they hear from afar, they disperse.
If they are not intimidated by the force of punishment (xíng shì),
And shaken by executions,
There is no way to control them.
This is the might of tyrannical scrutiny (bào chá zhī wēi).
What is meant by the "might of arrogant recklessness" (kuáng wàng zhī wēi)?
It means:
To have no heart for loving the people (ài rén zhī xīn).
To have no actions that benefit the people (lì rén zhī shì).
But daily to create ways to disrupt the people (luàn rén zhī dào).
When the people clamor and complain (xuān huá),
They are summarily arrested and subjected to torture (xíng zhuó).
It does not harmonize with the hearts of the people (hé rén xīn).
[Bèi nì tiānlǐ,] acting contrary to heavenly principles,
[shì yǐ shuǐhàn wèi zhī bùshí,] results in irregular floods and droughts,
[nián gǔ yǐ zhī bù shēng.] and consequently, crops fail to thrive.
[Bǎixìng shàng kùn yú bàoluàn zhī huàn,] The people above are plagued by the troubles of tyranny,
[ér xià qióng yīshí zhī yòng,] while below, they are impoverished and lack clothing and food.
[Chóu āi ér wú suǒ gàosù,] They are sorrowful and have no one to tell their woes to,
[bǐ zhōu fènkùi yǐ lí shàng,] forming factions and collapsing in resentment to break away from their superiors.
[Qīngfù mièwáng,] Overthrow and destruction
[kě lì ér dài.] can be awaited imminently.
[Shì kuángwàng zhī wēi yě.] This is the power of arrogance.
[Fū dàodé zhī wēi,] Now, the power of morality
[chéng hū zhòng qiáng.] is built upon the strength of the many.
[Bàochá zhī wēi,] The power of tyranny
[chéng hū wēi ruò.] is built upon weakness.
[Kuángwàng zhī wēi,] The power of arrogance
[chéng hū mièwáng.] is built upon destruction.
[Gù wēimíng tóng ér jíxiōng zhī xiào yuǎn yǐ.] Therefore, though the names of power are the same, the effects of good and bad are far apart.
[Gù bùkě bù shěnchá yě.] Thus, one must not fail to examine them carefully.
《Shī》yuē: The *Book of Poetry* says:
[Hàotiān jí wēi,] "Vast Heaven sends down its anger,
[tiān dǔ jiàng sàng,] Heaven truly sends down death and ruin,
[diàn wǒ jī jǐn,] Afflicting us with famine and drought,
[mín zú liúwáng." ] the people finally flee and perish."
6.27 Jìn Pínggōng, the Duke Píng of Jìn, was enjoying a pleasure trip on the river,
[yuē:] and said,
[Ān dé xiánshì yǔ zhī lè cǐ yě!] "How can I find a worthy scholar to enjoy this with me!"
[Chuán rén hé xū guì ér duì yuē:] A boatman, Hésū, knelt and replied,
[Zhǔjūn yì bù hǎo shì ěr.] "Our lord is simply not fond of scholars.
Now, pearls originate from rivers and seas,
and jade originates from the Kūnlún Mountains.
That they arrive without feet [on their own],
is because the ruler cherishes them.
That scholars have feet yet do not arrive,
is because the ruler has no intention of cherishing scholars.
There is no need to worry about not having scholars."
Píng Gōng said:
"I have one thousand retainers to the left of my gate,
and one thousand retainers to the right of my gate.
If the morning meal is insufficient,
I collect market taxes in the evening.
If the evening meal is insufficient,
I collect market taxes in the morning.
Can it be said that I do not cherish scholars?"
Hè Xū replied,
"Now, the swan in a single flight covers a thousand *lǐ*,
what it relies on is only its six flight feathers.
The feathers on its back,
the down on its belly,
adding a handful,
it will not fly any higher,
removing a handful,
it will not fly any lower.
Now, Your Lordship's retainers number one thousand to the left and one thousand to the right of your gate,
surely there are six flight feathers among them.
Or are they all feathers from the back and down from the belly?"
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"The planning men are exceedingly many,
therefore the matter is not accomplished."
Hàn Shī Wài Zhuàn, Volume 7
7.1 King Xuān of Qí said to Tián Guò:
"I have heard that the scholars mourn their parents for three years,
and mourn their ruler for three years.
Which is more important, the ruler or the father?"
Guò replied,
"I am afraid the father is more important."
The King angrily
said:
"Why do scholars leave their parents to serve their ruler?"
He replied:
"Without the ruler's land, there would be no place to settle my parents;
without the ruler's salary, there would be no way to support my parents;
without the ruler's rank and position, there would be no way to honor and glorify my parents.
I receive these from the ruler,
and give them to my parents.
All service to the ruler
is for the sake of my parents."
King Xuān looked displeased and had nothing to say in response.
The *Shī* says:
"The King's affairs are never-ending,
I have no time to escort my father."
7.2 The King of Zhào sent a man to Chǔ,
playing the *sè* as he sent him off,
saying:
"Be careful not to fail my words."
The envoy received the order,
and knelt without rising,
saying:
"The Great King has never played the *se* zither with such sorrow as today."
The king said:
"Indeed,
the *se* zither is indeed being tuned."
The envoy said:
"If it is being tuned, then one can record the positions of the bridges."
The king said:
"It is not possible.
The heavens have dryness and dampness,
the strings have looseness and tightness,
and the bridges have shifts,
so they cannot be recorded."
The envoy said:
"Please allow me to use this as an analogy.
The distance from Chǔ to Zhào is over a thousand *lǐ*,
and there are also changes of good and bad fortune.
If there is misfortune, then offer condolences;
if there is good fortune, then offer congratulations,
just as the bridges have shifts,
so they cannot be recorded.
Therefore, when an enlightened king sends someone on a mission,
he must be careful in choosing who he sends.
Once he has sent him,
he trusts him with his heart,
and not entrusting them with words.”
The *Shī* [Classic of Poetry] says:
“The marching soldiers hurry on,
Ever fearing they won't make it in time.”
This is probably lamenting the superiors’ control over their inferiors.
7.3 In Qí, there were hermits, Dōngguō Xiānshēng and Liáng Shíjūn.
When Cáo Xiàngguó was the chancellor of Qí,
a guest said to Kuì Shēng,
“These Dōngguō Xiānshēng and Liáng Shíjūn
are the worthies of this age.
They live in seclusion in the deep mountains,
and will never debase themselves and lower their ambitions to seek office.
I have heard that you, sir, are able to meet with Cáo Xiàngguó.
I wish you, sir, to pave the way for them.
The mother of my neighbor and I get along well.
The wife was suspected of stealing meat,
and her mother-in-law sent her away.
Filled with resentment, she complained to the mother of my neighbor.
The mother of my neighbor said,
‘Don’t worry.
I will now have the mother-in-law call you back.’
Immediately, she gathered firewood and went to the dismissed wife's house to ask for fire,
saying,
‘My dogs fought over meat and killed each other,
I am asking for fire to cook it.’
The mother-in-law then immediately sent someone to chase after the dismissed wife and bring her back.
Therefore, the mother of my neighbor was not a skilled orator,
To gather kindling and ask for fire
, is not the way to bring back a wife
, but things move people,
and events can be suitable.
Why not be the first to do it?”
Kuì Shēng 匱生 said:
“I fear my foolishness is insufficient.
However, I will try my best to gather kindling and ask for fire for Dōngguō Xiānshēng 東郭先生 and Liáng Shíjūn 梁石君.”
Thereupon he went to see Chancellor Cáo 曹, saying:
"In my village, there are those who marry three days after their husband's death
, and there are those who never marry their whole lives.
If you were to take a wife yourself,
whom would you choose?"
The Chancellor said:
"I would also marry one who never marries for life."
Kuì Shēng 匱生 said:
"In Qí 齊 there are hermits, Dōngguō Xiānshēng 東郭先生 and Liáng Shíjūn 梁石君,
virtuous scholars of the age.
They dwell in the deep mountains
and will never humble themselves to seek office.
When the Chancellor takes a wife
, he desires to marry one who does not marry
; why, when choosing ministers, would you not choose ministers who do not serve?"
Thereupon, Chancellor Cáo 曹, through Kuì Shēng 匱生, used bundles of silk and a comfortable carriage to welcome Dōngguō Xiānshēng 東郭先生 and Liáng Shíjūn 梁石君
and treated them generously.
The *Shī* 詩 [Book of Odes] says:
"Now that I have seen the prince,
my heart is at peace."
7.4 Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the past, the Duke of Zhōu served King Wén,
acting without arbitrary decisions,
handling affairs without personal inclination,
his body appearing as if unable to bear the weight of his clothes,
his words seeming as if reluctant to leave his mouth,
always having someone to support him from the front,
being cautious, as if about to lose something.
He could be called a filial son.
When King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young,
the Duke of Zhōu carried on the work of Kings Wén and Wǔ,
assumed the position of the Son of Heaven,
listened to the government affairs of the Son of Heaven,
quelled the rebellions of the Ì and Dí tribes,
punished the crimes of Guǎn and Cài,
held King Chéng and held court with the feudal lords,
making judgments on punishment and rewards,
without consulting anyone,
his power moved heaven and earth,
his awe shook the whole country.
He could be called skilled in military affairs.
When King Chéng grew up,
the Duke of Zhōu returned the government,
faced north and served him as a subject,
acting only after requesting permission,
without any display of boasting or pride.
He could be called a capable minister.
Therefore, for one person's character,
to be capable of three changes
is how one responds to the times."
The *Shī* says:
"Turning to the left, turning to the left,
the jūnzi deems it appropriate;
turning to the right, turning to the right,
the jūnzi possesses it."
7.5 The *Zhuàn* says:
"Birds with beautiful feathers and hooked beaks,
birds fear them.
Fish with large mouths and drooping fat,
fish fear them.
People with sharp mouths and eloquent words,
people fear them."
Therefore, the jūnzi avoids three extremes:
avoids the brush of the literati,
avoids the sharp point of the warrior,
avoids the tongue of the debater.
The *Shī* says:
"I treat my friends with reverence!
Slander will arise."
7.6 Kǒngzǐ, trapped between Chén and Cài,
set out his three classics on a mat.
For seven days he had nothing to eat,
not even grain to thicken his léi broth.
His disciples showed signs of hunger,
but he continued reading the *Shū* and practicing rituals and music.
Zǐ Lù stepped forward to remonstrate, saying:
"Those who do good,
Heaven rewards them with blessings.
Those who do evil,
Heaven repays them with calamity.
Now, Master, you have accumulated virtue and piled up benevolence,
having done good for a long time.
I suspect there is still some oversight,
some hidden place where you remain?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, come here!
You are a small man,
not versed in discussion.
Stay,
I will tell you.
Do you think the wise are without guilt?
Then why did Prince Bǐ Gān have his heart cut out and die?
Do you think the righteous are heeded?
Then why did Wǔ Zǐxū have his eyes gouged out and hung on the east gate of Wú?
Do you think the incorruptible are employed?
Then why did Bó Yí and Shū Qí starve on Shǒuyáng Mountain?
Do you think the loyal are employed?
Then why was Bào Shū not employed?
Lord Yè Gōngzǐ Gāo never served in office his whole life,
Bào Jiāo hugged a tree and wept,
Zǐ Tuī climbed a mountain and burned to death?
Therefore, gentlemen with extensive learning and deep planning,
many do not meet with the times.
How could it be just me, Qiū (丘)?
Being worthy or unworthy is a matter of talent (cái 也).
Meeting with fortune or not is a matter of timing (shí 時).
Now that there is no opportunity (shí 時),
where can the worthy be employed?
Therefore, Yú Shùn (虞舜) tilled the land on the sunny side of Mount Lì,
and was established as the Son of Heaven,
which was his meeting with Yáo (堯).
Fù Yuè (傅說) carried earth and built walls,
and was made a high official,
which was his meeting with Wǔ Dīng (武丁).
Yī Yǐn (伊尹) was originally a servant of the House of Xīn (莘氏),
carrying cauldrons and holding chopping boards, adjusting the five flavors,
and was established as prime minister,
which was his meeting with Tāng (湯).
Lǚ Wàng (呂望), at the age of fifty,
sold food at Jí Jīn (棘津),
and at the age of seventy, butchered in Zhāo Gē (朝歌).
At ninety, he became the teacher of the Son of Heaven,
which was his meeting with King Wén (文王).
Guǎn Yíwú (管夷吾), bound and shackled, from within a prison cart,
was made Zhòng Fù (仲父),
which was his meeting with Duke Qí Huán (齊桓公).
Bǎi Lǐxī (百里奚) sold himself for the price of five sheepskins,
and herded cattle for the Duke of Qín (秦伯),
and was promoted to high official,
which was his meeting with Duke Qín Mù (秦繆公).
Yú Qiū (虞丘)'s name was known throughout the world,
He was considered for the position of *lìngyǐn* (prime minister),
but yielded it to Sūn Shū'áo 孫叔敖.
Such was his encounter with King Zhuāng of Chǔ 楚莊王.
Wǔ Zǐxū's 伍子胥 earlier achievements were numerous,
but later he was cruelly put to death.
It was not that he understood the waxing and waning of fortune;
earlier he encountered Hélǘ 闔閭,
later he encountered Fūchāi 夫差.
A fine horse pulling a salt cart becomes exhausted.
This is not because it lacks its proper form,
but because no one recognizes it.
If a fine horse does not encounter Bólè 伯樂,
how could it attain its thousand-lǐ legs?
Zàofù 造父 also would not have his thousand-lǐ hands.
Orchids and zhǐ (a fragrant herb) grow in the midst of lush forests,
in the depths of mountains.
Because people rarely see them, they are not fragrant.
The purpose of study is not to achieve worldly success.
It is to be free from distress in poverty,
to maintain one's will without decline in sorrow,
to know in advance the beginning of misfortune and fortune,
and to have no confusion in one's heart.
Therefore, the sage lives in seclusion and contemplates deeply,
hearing and seeing in solitude.
Shùn 舜 was also a wise sage.
He faced south and governed the world,
solely because he encountered Yáo 堯.
If Shùn lived in the era of Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂,
If one can save oneself from punishment and execution,
that is already good.
What need is there for a high position?
Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
At those times,
was it that Guān Lóngpáng lacked wisdom,
or that Prince Bǐgān was not intelligent?
They all simply did not meet the right time.
Therefore, the gentleman strives to learn,
cultivates himself, rectifies his conduct, and awaits his time.
Do not be confused by this."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"The crane cries in the marsh,
its voice is heard in the heavens."
7.7 Zēngzǐ said:
"What is gone and cannot return is one's parents.
What has arrived and cannot be added to is one's age.
Therefore, the filial son desires to provide for them,
but his parents do not wait for him.
The wood desires to be straight,
but the time does not wait for it.
Therefore, sacrificing an ox at the grave
is not as good as offering chicken and pork while the parents are still alive.
Thus, I once served as an official in Qí,
and my salary was no more than a *zhōng* or *fǔ*.
Yet, I was still delighted and happy,
not because I thought it was much,
He rejoiced in being able to provide for his parents.
After they had passed away,
I once traveled south to Chǔ,
and obtained a high-ranking official position there.
My hall was nine *rèn* tall,
the rafters were three spans in circumference,
and the carriages that turned their axles numbered a hundred.
Yet, I still faced north and wept tears,
not because I was in a lowly position,
but because I grieved that I could no longer provide for my parents."
Therefore, if one's family is poor and one's parents are old, one should not be picky about official positions but take office.
As for those who prioritize their own ambitions
and neglect their parents,
they are not filial.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"When there is a mother, the body is at peace."
7.8 Zhào Jiǎnzi 赵简子 had a retainer named Zhōu Shě 周舍,
who stood below the gate for three days and three nights.
Jiǎnzi 赵简子 sent someone to ask him,
saying:
"What business do you have with me that you wish to see me?"
Zhōu Shě 周舍 replied:
"I wish to be a frank and outspoken minister,
holding a black brush and a writing tablet,
following behind you,
recording your mistakes and writing them down,
so that there is a record every day,
an accomplishment every month,
years is effective."
Jiǎn Zǐ was pleased and when at home, he would stay with him;
when going out, he would go out with him.
After not many days,
Zhōu Shè died.
Jiǎn Zǐ mourned as if he had lost a son.
Later, he was drinking with the various senior officials at the Hóngbō Terrace,
and when the wine was flowing,
Jiǎn Zǐ wept.
The senior officials all fled,
saying,
"Your servant has committed a crime but is unaware of it."
Jiǎn Zǐ said,
"The senior officials are all without fault.
In the past, I had Zhōu Shè who said,
'The hide of a thousand sheep is not as good as the fur from one fox's armpit;
the agreement of many people is not as good as the honest and upright speech of one scholar.'
In the past, Shāng Zhòu was silent and perished;
Wǔ Wáng spoke frankly and prospered.
Now, since the death of Zhōu Shè,
I have not heard of my faults.
My ruin will not be long in coming.
This is why I, the寡人 (guǎrén, a term used by rulers to refer to themselves), am weeping."
7.9 The *Commentary* says:
Qí Jǐng Gōng asked Yàn Zǐ:
"What is the worry for a state?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"I am troubled by the shrine rat."
Jǐng Gōng said, "
What is meant by 'shrine rat'?"
Yàn Zǐ said, "
The shrine rat goes out to steal from the outside,
and comes in to take refuge in the shrine.
If we flood it, we fear damaging the wall;
if we smoke it out, we fear burning the wood.
This is the trouble with shrine rats.
Now, those around you, my lord,
when they go out, sell you to demand profit;
when they come in, they rely on you.
They are not punished though they disrupt the law,
and you even shelter and nurture them.
This is the trouble with shrine rats."
Jǐng Gōng said, "
Alas,
could it be so!"
"There was a man who sold wine in the market, and his wine was very good.
He placed a very long marker,
yet the wine turned sour and did not sell.
He asked the people in the neighborhood the reason.
The people in the neighborhood said,
'Your dog is very fierce,
and when people carry vessels and want to go there,
the dog always comes out to bite them,
and that is why the wine has turned sour and does not sell.'
When a scholar wants to advise the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
Those in power who come forward to bite people are
also the vicious dogs of the state.
Those on the left and right are the rats of the shrines,
those in power are the vicious dogs;
this is a great calamity for the state."
The "Book of Odes" says:
"Look at that central forest,
preparing firewood and offerings."
It speaks of the court being full of petty people.
7.10 In the past, Sīchéng Zǐhàn, as minister of Sòng,
said to the ruler of Sòng:
"The safety and danger of the state,
the order and disorder of the people,
lie in Your Majesty's execution of rewards and punishments.
Now, titles and salaries, rewards and gifts,
are what the people like;
Your Majesty should carry them out yourself.
Slaughter and executions,
are what the people hate;
your servant asks to take them on."
The ruler of Sòng said:
"Good.
I will take the good parts,
and you take the bad;
I know that I will not be laughed at by the feudal lords."
The people of the state knew that the execution of slaughter rested entirely with Zǐhàn,
so the high officials became intimate with him,
The common people feared him.
In less than a year,
Zǐ Hǎn consequently drove out the ruler of Sòng and monopolized the government.
Therefore, the *Lǎozi* says:
"Fish cannot be taken out of the deep pool;
the sharp weapons of the state cannot be shown to the people."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Why did you appoint me,
without consulting me?"
7.11 During the time of Duke Yì of Wèi,
there was a minister named Hóng Yǎn,
who received an order to go on a mission.
Before he returned,
the Dí people attacked Wèi.
Thereupon, Duke Yì wanted to raise an army to meet them.
All the people said:
"Those whom the ruler values and who have positions and stipends,
are the cranes.
Those whom he loves,
are the palace women.
Let the cranes and palace women also fight.
How can we fight!"
Consequently, they collapsed and all fled.
The Dí people arrived,
and attacked Duke Yì at Yíngzé,
killing him.
They completely ate his flesh,
leaving only his liver.
Hóng Yǎn arrived,
and reported the mission to the liver.
After finishing his address,
he cried out to Heaven.
When his lamentation ceased,
he said:
"For a servant like me,
death alone is sufficient."
Thereupon, he disemboweled himself,
took out his abdominal contents,
and placed the liver of Yì Gōng inside [his abdomen],
and then died.
Duke Huán heard of this
and said:
"The fall of Wèi was
due to its lack of principle.
Now that it has a minister such as this,
it cannot but be preserved."
Thereupon, he re-established Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Like Hóng Yǎn,
he can be called a loyal officer.
He sacrificed his life to save his lord,
and not only did he save his lord,
but he also caused the ancestral temples of Wèi to be re-established
and the sacrifices to continue without interruption;
he can be said to have performed a great service.
The *Shī* says:
"Everywhere there is ease,
I dwell alone in sorrow.
The people are all prosperous,
I alone dare not rest."
7.12 Sūn Shū'áo met the old man of Fox Mound.
The old man of Fox Mound said:
"I have heard that
a man with three benefits must have three misfortunes.
Do you know this?"
Sūn Shū'áo changed his expression with respect and said:
"I am not clever enough,
how could I possibly know it?
May I ask what are the three benefits?
What are the three misfortunes?"
The old man of Fox Mound said:
"Those whose rank is high,
people envy them.
Those whose office is great,
the ruler dislikes them.
Those whose salary is generous,
resentment is directed towards them.
This is what is meant."
Sūn Shū'áo said:
"Not so.
The higher my rank becomes,
the lower my ambition goes.
The greater my office becomes,
the smaller my heart becomes.
The more generous my salary becomes,
My bestowals of favor are extensive.
Can I avoid misfortune?"
The old man of Húqiū said:
"Excellent words!
Even Yáo and Shùn were still troubled by these things."
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Gentle and respectful people,
gather like [birds] on a tree.
Anxious and careful,
as if facing a deep valley."
7.13 Confucius said:
"Enlightened rulers have three fears.
The first is being in a position of honor but fearing not hearing their faults.
The second is being successful but fearing arrogance.
The third is hearing the ultimate Way of the world but fearing not being able to practice it.
Formerly, King Gōujiàn of Yuè fought against Wú,
greatly defeated them,
and also possessed the Southern Yi.
At that time,
the ruler stood facing south,
with three close ministers,
and five distant ministers,
and ordered the high officials, saying:
'Those who hear of my faults but do not inform me will be punished most severely.'
This is an example of being in a position of honor but fearing not hearing their faults.
Formerly, Duke Wén of Jìn fought against Chǔ,
greatly defeated them,
burned their grass,
The fire burned for three days without ceasing.
Duke Wén retired with a worried expression.
An attendant said,
"Your Lordship has greatly defeated Chǔ, yet you look worried.
Why is that?"
Duke Wén said,
"I have heard that only a sage can win a battle and remain at peace!
As for those who win by deceit,
they are never not in danger.
That is why I am worried."
This is being afraid of arrogance despite achieving one's ambition.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng and stood facing south.
Duke Huán said,
"Having obtained these two men,
my eyes are clearer,
my ears are sharper.
I dare not monopolize them,
but present them to my ancestors."
This is hearing the ultimate principle and fearing one's inability to put it into practice.
Judging from Duke Huán of Qí, Duke Wén of Jìn, and King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè,
these three fears
are the duties of an enlightened ruler."
The *Book of Odes* says,
"Kind and respectful is the person,
as if alighting on a tree.
Anxious and cautious,
as if standing by a deep valley.
Trembling and apprehensive,
"Like treading on thin ice."
This saying applies to Your Majesty, who is in a position above others.
7.14 King Zhuāng of Chǔ bestowed wine upon his ministers.
As dusk fell and the wine flowed freely,
all those around him became intoxicated.
The candles in the hall were extinguished,
and someone pulled on the Queen's sleeve.
The Queen grabbed at the string of his cap and broke it off,
then said to the King:
"Now that the candles are out,
someone pulled on my sleeve,
and I grabbed at the string of his cap and broke it off.
I wish you would light a fire to see who broke their cap string."
The King said:
"Stop!"
He immediately issued an order, saying:
"Today, those who drink with me,
if they do not break their cap string,
will not be considered to be enjoying themselves."
Consequently, none of the cap strings remained intact,
and no one knew who had broken the Queen's cap string.
Thereupon, the King continued to drink happily with his ministers
and then dismissed them.
Later, when the army of Wú rose up and attacked Chǔ,
there was a man who constantly responded and fought in unison,
charging into the enemy formation five times, repelling them,
and finally taking the head of the enemy's general and presenting it.
The king, finding this strange, asked him, saying:
"I, your sovereign, have never treated you differently from others.
Why do you favor me so greatly?"
He replied:
"Your servant is the one who cut the tassel from his hat at the palace banquet.
At that time, I should have given my all, even to the point of death.
I have been indebted to you for a long time
without having accomplished anything for you.
Now I am fortunate to be employed by you. According to my sense of duty,
I can still help Your Majesty defeat Wú and strengthen Chǔ."
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"There is a deep pool,
where reeds and rushes grow densely."
This speaks of how a great person is all-encompassing.
7.15 The *Zhuàn* [Commentary] says:
Bó Qí was filial but was abandoned by his father.
Yǐn Gōng was benevolent but was killed by his younger brother.
Shū Wǔ was virtuous but was killed by his elder brother.
Bǐ Gān was loyal but was executed by his ruler.
The *Shī* [Book of Poetry] says:
"I am carefully innocent."
7.16 Zhòu killed Prince Bǐ Gān,
and Jī Zǐ let his hair down and feigned madness.
Chén Líng Gōng killed Xiè Yě,
and Dèng Yuán left Chén with his clan to follow [someone else].
After this,
Yīn was annexed by Zhōu,
Chén was destroyed by Chǔ
because it killed Bǐ Gān and Xiè Yě,
and lost Jī Zǐ and Dèng Yuán.
When King Zhāo of Yān acquired Guō Wěi, Zōu Yǎn and Yuè Yì came from Qí and Wèi of their own accord.
Consequently, Wèi and Zhào raised troops to attack Qí,
forcing King Mǐn to take refuge in Jǔ.
The territory and population of Yān
were not equal to those of Qí.
However, the reason why people believed in Yān to such an extent
was due to obtaining talented individuals.
Therefore, there is no perpetually secure state.
There are no people perpetually easy to govern.
Those who obtain the virtuous prosper,
those who lose the virtuous perish.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been an exception.
Now, a clear mirror
is for reflecting one's form.
The past
is for understanding the present.
If one knows the reasons for the peril and destruction of the past,
but does not strive to follow the ways of security and preservation,
then there is no difference from walking backwards while trying to catch up to the people in front.
Tài Gōng understood this,
so he promoted the descendants of Wēi Zǐ and honored the tomb of Bǐ Gān.
The sages' treatment of the descendants of the virtuous
was so generous,
how much more so should their treatment of the virtuous who are still alive in their own time?
The *Shī*
says: "Hàotiān is so vast,
I am careful not to harm the innocent."
7.17 Sòng Yù, through his friend, was presented to King Xiāng of Chǔ.
King Xiāng treated him no differently from others,
so Sòng Yù blamed his friend.
The friend said:
"Ginger and cinnamon grow because of the ground,
but they are not spicy because of the ground.
A woman marries through a matchmaker,
but she is not intimate because of the matchmaker.
You have not served the king yet,
why do you resent me?"
Sòng Yù said:
"Not so.
In the past, Qí had a cunning rabbit
that could run five hundred *lǐ* in a day.
If you only point and look at it,
even a good dog cannot catch up to the dust of the cunning rabbit.
But if you hold its collar and release the leash,
then even Dōngguō Juān could not leave it.
Now, the way you have introduced me,
are you following its tracks and releasing the leash?
Or are you just pointing and looking at it?"
The *Shī* says:
"To seek peace and happiness,
abandon me and make me forgotten."
7.18 Sòng Yàn, serving as minister of Qí, was dismissed and driven out.
Upon returning to his residence,
he summoned the gate warden Chén Ráo 陳饒 and twenty-five others,
and said:
"Are there any of you gentlemen who can go with me to join the feudal lords?"
Chén Ráo 陳饒 and the others all prostrated themselves and did not answer.
Sòng Yàn 宋燕 said:
"Alas!
How easy it is to obtain scholar-officials, yet how difficult it is to employ them!"
Ráo 饒 said:
"It is not that scholar-officials are easy to obtain and difficult to employ,
but rather that you, my lord, are unable to employ them.
If you are unable to employ them,
then they will harbor feelings of discontent.
This is losing it yourself and blaming others."
Sòng Yàn 宋燕 said:
"What do you mean by losing it oneself and blaming others?"
Chén Ráo 陳饒 said:
"Three *dǒu* of millet is insufficient for a soldier,
yet your geese and ducks have surplus grain;
this is one fault of yours, my lord.
The fruits in the orchards, pears and chestnuts,
are used by the women of the inner palace to throw at each other,
yet the soldiers have never had a taste of them;
this is the second fault of yours, my lord.
Fine silks and gauzes,
lavishly adorn the halls,
and are ruined by the wind,
yet the soldiers have never had any to use as hems;
This is your third transgression.
Moreover, wealth
is what you, my lord, consider light.
Death
is what warriors consider heavy.
You cannot enact what you consider light,
and yet you want to make warriors give their all, which they consider heavy.
This is like keeping a lead knife as a pet
and expecting it to be used like a Gān Jiàng sword.
Wouldn't that be difficult?"
Sòng Yàn’s face showed a look of shame.
Hesitantly, he left his seat and said,
"This is Yàn's fault."
The *Book of Odes* says:
"Some offer their wine,
but not their thin gruel."
7.19 The *Commentary* says:
Those who are good at governing
follow the appropriateness of feelings and nature,
follow the order of *yīn* and *yáng*,
understand the principle of root and branch,
and unite the boundaries of Heaven and humanity.
If this is done, then the weather will reverently nourish, and living things will flourish beautifully.
Those who do not know how to govern
cause feelings to be satiated with nature,
cause *yīn* to overcome *yáng*,
cause the branch to go against the root,
and cause people to deceive Heaven.
When the vital energy is suppressed and not trusted,
stifled and not released,
in such a case, disasters arise,
strange phenomena occur,
all living things are harmed,
and the year's harvest is not ripe.
Therefore, its movement injures virtue,
its stillness loses salvation.
Thus, those who are slow attend to it,
those who are hasty do not understand it,
daily acting contrary to principle and yet desiring to achieve order.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Abandonment becomes ruin and robbery,
none know the cause."
7.20 During the time of Wèi Wénhóu,
Zǐ Zhì served as an official and incurred punishment,
left and traveled north,
and said to Jiǎnzhǔ:
"From now on,
I will no longer cultivate virtue in people."
Jiǎnzhǔ said:
"Why?"
Zhì said:
"Of those I have cultivated, half are gentlemen in the hall,
half are high officials in the court,
and half are people on the border.
Now, the gentlemen in the hall
fear me because of the law,
"The people on the border use weapons to rob us,
thus they do not establish virtue among the people."
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
"Alas!
Your words are excessive.
In spring, plant peach and plum trees;
in summer, you can find shade beneath them;
in autumn, you can eat their fruit.
In spring, plant tribulus;
in summer, you cannot gather its leaves;
in autumn, you get its thorns.
From this, we can see that
it lies in what is planted.
Now, what you have planted
is not the right person,
therefore, a gentleman chooses first and then plants."
The *Shī* says:
"Do not move a large cart,
lest the dust rises dimly."
7.21 An upright person follows the correct path in their actions,
speaks according to reason,
is fair, just, and selfless,
does not indulge their will in times of ease,
and does not act rashly in times of danger.
In the past, when Wèi Xiàn Gōng fled into exile,
upon returning to the country and reaching the outskirts of the capital,
he intended to bestow estates upon his followers before entering.
The Grand Historian Liǔ Zhuāng said:
"If everyone guards the altars of the state,
then who will bear the burden of traveling and following [the prince]?
If everyone follows,
then who will guard the altars of the state?
The prince returning to the state and acting selfishly,
isn't that unacceptable?"
Therefore, he did not distribute the spoils.
Liǔ Zhuāng (柳莊) was upright.
In the past, the senior minister Shǐ Yú (史魚) of Wèi (衛) was ill and about to die.
He said to his son:
"I repeatedly spoke of the worthiness of Qú Bóyù (蘧伯玉) but could not advance him,
and the unworthiness of Mí Zixiá (彌子瑕) but could not remove him.
As a minister, failing to advance the worthy and remove the unworthy in life,
upon death, I should not have my funeral arranged in the main hall.
Bury me in a room; that will be enough."
The ruler of Wèi (衛) asked the reason for this.
His son reported his father's words.
The ruler, startled, summoned Qú Bóyù (蘧伯玉) and honored him,
and dismissed Mí Zixiá (彌子瑕),
and moved the coffin to the main hall,
completing the rituals before leaving.
He admonished with his person in life,
and admonished with his corpse in death;
he can be called upright.
The *Shī* (詩) [Book of Odes] says:
"Reverently attend to your position,
and love that which is upright."
7.22 Kǒngzǐ (孔子) was at leisure,
Zǐ Gòng was sitting in attendance,
and asked, "What is the Way of being a subordinate?"
Confucius said,
"Excellent!
Your question!
To be a subordinate,
it is perhaps like earth."
Zǐ Gòng did not understand.
Confucius said,
"Earth is such that
if you dig it, you obtain sweet springs;
if you plant in it, you obtain the five grains;
grasses and trees are planted in it;
birds, beasts, fish, and turtles thrive in it.
When alive, one stands upon it;
when dead, one enters it;
it performs many services without speaking;
and its benefits to the world never cease.
Therefore, it is said:
'He who can be a subordinate,
he is perhaps like earth!'"
Zǐ Gòng said,
"Though Cì is not clever,
I will put this saying into practice."
The *Shī* says:
"In setting the standard of ritual, let there be no fault."
7.23 The *Zhuàn* says:
Běn, the son of Nán Jiǎ, was passing through Chéng,
He cooked *lǐ* fish for him.
Nán Jiǎzǐ said,
"I have heard that gentlemen do not eat *lǐ* fish."
Běn Zǐ said,
"This is something gentlemen do not eat,
what does it have to do with me?"
Jiǎzǐ said,
"Elevated comparisons are how virtue is broadened,
and inferior comparisons are how conduct is narrowed.
Comparing oneself to the good
is a step towards advancement.
Comparing oneself to the evil
is the source of one's decline.
Moreover, doesn't the *Book of Poetry* say:
'High mountains are looked up to,
Great roads are travelled on.'
How could I compare myself to a gentleman?
I only aspire to it."
7.24 Zǐgòng asked about great ministers.
Confucius said,
"In Qí there was Bào Shū,
and in Zhèng there was Zǐpí."
Zǐgòng said,
"No.
In Qí there was Guǎn Zhòng,
and in Zhèng there was Dōnglǐ Zǐchǎn."
Confucius said,
"*Chǎn* recommended them."
Zǐ Gòng said:
"If that's the case, then recommend those who are virtuous from among the virtuous."
(Confucius) said:
"To recognize the virtuous
is wisdom (zhì yě).
To promote the virtuous
is benevolence (rén yě).
To employ the virtuous
is righteousness (yì yě).
Having these three,
what more is needed?"
7.25 Kǒngzǐ was traveling on Jǐng Mountain,
Zǐ Lù, Zǐ Gòng, and Yán Yuān followed.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When a gentleman ascends to a high place, he is sure to compose poetry.
Little ones, express your wishes;
what would you say your wishes are?
I, Qiū, shall enlighten you."
Zǐ Lù said:
"Yóu wishes to brandish a long halberd, to sweep through the three armies,
with a fierce tiger at my back,
and enemies before me,
like a dragon leaping and a jiao dragon rising up,
to advance and rescue the calamities of two nations."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A brave warrior indeed!"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"When two nations engage in conflict,
Strong warriors arrayed in battle formation,
dust and dirt rising to fill the sky,
Cì (賜) would not carry a single foot of weapon,
or a single *dǒu* of grain,
yet resolve the difficulties of two nations.
Those who employ Cì will survive,
those who do not employ Cì will perish."
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"A debater indeed!"
Yán Huí (顏回) was unwilling.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"Why are you unwilling, Huí (回)?"
Yán Yuān (顏淵) said,
"The two gentlemen have already expressed their willingness,
therefore I dare not express my own."
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"It is not the same;
our intentions each have their own purpose.
Huí (回), express your willingness;
I, Qiū (丘), will enlighten you."
Yán Yuān (顏淵) said,
"I wish to obtain a small state and assist it.
The ruler would govern with the Dao (道),
the ministers would transform through virtue,
ruler and ministers would be of one mind,
external and internal affairs would correspond.
The feudal lords of the various states
would all follow righteousness and turn towards the wind (of virtue),
The strong hurried forward,
the old were helped along.
Instruction was practiced among the people,
virtue extended to the four barbarian tribes.
None did not lay down their weapons,
converging like spokes on a hub at the four gates.
The world all obtained lasting peace,
even buzzing flies and wriggling creatures
each enjoyed their nature.
Talented people were advanced, the able were employed,
each was entrusted with their tasks.
Thereupon, the ruler found peace above,
the ministers were harmonious below,
ruling by non-action,
acting always according to the Dao,
leisurely attaining ritual propriety.
Those who spoke of benevolence and righteousness were rewarded,
those who spoke of war and strife were put to death.
Then, from what does Yóu gain to save?
By what gift is difficulty resolved?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A sage indeed!
When a great man appears,
small men hide.
When a sage arises,
the worthy lie low.
If I, Huí, were in charge,
how could I possibly bring my abilities to bear compared to Cì?"
The *Shī*
'The rain and snow fall heavily,
But when the sun appears, they melt away.'"
7.26 In the past, Kǒngzǐ played the zither,
and Zēngzǐ and Zǐgòng listened outside the door.
When the music ended,
Zēngzǐ said,
"Alas!
The Master's zither playing seems to have the ambition of a greedy wolf [tānláng zhī zhì],
and the conduct of wickedness and depravity [xiépì zhī xíng].
How extremely unkind and profit-seeking it is!"
Zǐgòng thought this was correct,
and without replying, went inside.
The Master saw that Zǐgòng had the look of one who would admonish him for his faults,
and the appearance of one who would raise objections,
so he put down the zither and waited for him.
Zǐgòng told him what Zēngzǐ had said.
The Master said,
"Alas!
That Cān,
is a worthy man in the world,
and he is skilled at recognizing musical tones.
Just now, when I was playing the zither,
a mouse came out to play,
a wildcat appeared on the roof,
walking stealthily along the beam,
approaching and then hiding,
lowering its eyes and arching its back,
To seek and not obtain.
Qiū used the zither to indulge in licentious music.
Cān considered Qiū to be greedy, savage, and deviant,
isn't that suitable!"
The *Shī* says:
"Drums and bells are struck in the palace,
their sound is heard outside."
7.27 Furthermore, one who is a father,
must cherish compassionate love,
to nurture his son.
To caress and nourish with food and drink,
to preserve his body.
When he comes to have knowledge,
he must dwell solemnly and speak rightly,
to guide him forward.
When he comes of age to bind his hair,
entrust him to a wise teacher to perfect his skill.
At nineteen, when he makes his intentions known,
invite a guest to crown him,
sufficient to fulfill his aspirations.
When his blood and qi are clear and calm,
engage a wife within to settle him,
faithfully accept the parental teachings,
without any doubts.
Do not scold the capped son,
do not whip the haired son,
heed his subtle advice,
do not cause him worry.
This is the way of being a father.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Father, you gave me life;
Mother, you nurtured me.
You caressed me, you fed me;
You raised me, you educated me;
You cared for me, you protected me;
Going out, coming in, you held me in your arms."
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, Volume 8.
8.1 Yuè Wáng Gōujiàn sent Lián Jī to present people to the Jīng King.
The Jīng King's envoy said:
"Yuè
is a state of uncivilized barbarians.
I request to deceive their envoy."
The Jīng King said:
"The King of Yuè
is a wise man;
his envoy is also wise.
You must be careful."
The envoy went out to see Lián Jī and
said:
"If you wear a hat, you can be seen according to custom.
If you do not wear a hat, you cannot be seen."
Lián Jī said:
"Yuè is also one of the states enfeoffed by the Zhōu Dynasty.
Not able to be situated in a great country,
but situated along the shores of the rivers and seas,
He lived alongside fish and turtles.
He tattooed his body and cut his hair before settling there.
Now, having arrived in the superior kingdom,
you insist that unless I wear the proper headwear, I will not be granted an audience,
and without the headwear, I cannot be seen.
If this is the case,
then if an envoy from the superior kingdom were to go to Yuè,
would he also have to cut off his nose, tattoo his body, and cut his hair before being granted an audience,
is that acceptable?"
When the King of Jīng heard this,
he threw on his clothes and went out to apologize.
Confucius said,
"To be an envoy in the four directions
and not disgrace the ruler's mandate,
can be called a shì."
8.2 People cherish wealth, honor, and ease,
and being praised by others,
all for the sake of their own bodies.
They detest poverty, lowliness, danger, and disgrace,
and being slandered by others,
also for the sake of their own bodies.
But what is so precious about the body?
Nothing is more precious than one's qì (vital energy).
People gain life from qì,
and lose life when they lose qì.
This qì is not gold, silk, pearls, or jade;
it cannot be obtained from others.
It is not silk cloth or the five grains;
It cannot be obtained by purchasing it.
It resides within oneself.
One must be careful.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Being both perceptive and wise,
Preserve yourself."
8.3 When the people of Wú 吳 attacked Chǔ 楚,
King Zhāo 昭 fled the state.
A butcher, Yuè 說, followed him.
When King Zhāo 昭 returned to the state,
He rewarded those who had followed him.
When it came to Yuè 說,
Yuè 說 declined, saying:
"When the ruler lost the state,
What this subject lost was only his butchering business.
When the ruler returned to the state,
This subject also returned to his butchering.
The compensation I received is already generous.
What reward should there be?"
He declined to accept the order.
The ruler insisted,
Yuè 說 said:
"The ruler lost the state,
It was not this subject's fault,
Therefore I dared not submit to punishment.
The ruler returned to the state,
It was not this subject's merit,
Therefore I dare not accept the reward.
When the Wú 吳 army entered Yǐng 郢,
I, your servant, feared the enemy and avoided calamity.
Now that you, my lord, have returned to the state,
what matter is there for me to discuss?"
The ruler said,
"If you do not accept, then I will see you."
Yuè Shuō 說 replied,
"The law of the Chǔ 楚 state is that
if a merchant wishes to see the ruler,
he must have a great gift and substantial collateral
before he can be received.
Now, my wisdom was not able to preserve the state,
my integrity was not able to die for the ruler,
my courage was not able to withstand the enemy.
Yet, to be received
would be against the law of the state."
Thereupon, he did not accept the command
and entered into a mountain stream.
King Zhāo 昭 of Chǔ said to Sīmǎ Zǐqī 司馬子期,
"There is a man here
whose dwelling is very simple,
whose discussions are very lofty.
Find him for me.
I wish to be as brothers with him
and would like to appoint him as one of the three highest ministers."
Sīmǎ Zǐqī abandoned his chariot and retinue to seek him out.
After five days and five nights,
he found him
Someone said:
"To not save a country in danger
is not rén (仁, benevolence).
To not obey the ruler's orders
is not zhōng (忠, loyalty).
To despise wealth and nobility above,
and relish poverty and hardship below,
this intention is a fault.
Now the ruler wishes to be brothers
and offers you the position of one of the Three Dukes.
You do not listen to the ruler.
Why?"
Tú Yángzǐ (屠羊子) replied:
"The position of the Three Dukes, I know it is more esteemed than a butcher's stall.
A ten-thousand-zhong salary (萬鍾之祿), I know it is richer than the profit from butchering sheep.
To see the benefit of rank and salary now,
and forget the proper etiquette of declining it,
is something I have not heard of."
Thereupon he declined the position of the Three Dukes
and returned to his butcher's stall.
A jūnzǐ (君子, gentleman) who heard of this said:
"How extreme!
The actions of Tú Yángzǐ.
He constrains himself, endures poverty, and dwells in the land of others."
Tú Yángzǐ said:
"What do you mean by 'poverty'?
I yielded to him with propriety, and (thereby) completed his country."
The gentleman said:
"To be in a deep abyss and not aid others in their peril,
to see Zhāo Wáng's 昭王 virtue decline in Wú 吳,
and to hoard treasures while cutting off all traces,
thereby harming the country,
is to desire to preserve only oneself.
This is being generous to oneself and stingy to one's ruler,
making one a self-seeking and not a savior of the world."
"What, then, can be called saving the world?"
He said:
"People like Shēn Bó 申伯 and Zhòng Shānfǔ 仲山甫 can be called saviors of the world.
In the past, when the virtue of the Zhōu 周 dynasty greatly declined,
and the Way was abandoned under Lì 厲,
Shēn Bó 申伯 and Zhòng Shānfǔ 仲山甫 assisted and supported King Xuān 宣王,
correcting the chaotic world and turning it back to righteousness,
and the realm was slightly revitalized,
and the ancestral temples were restored.
Shēn Bó 申伯 and Zhòng Shānfǔ 仲山甫 then conformed to the desires of the world,
correcting errors and saving those who had lost their way,
explaining virtue and teachings,
promoting neglected scholars,
and the whole country harmoniously turned to them like the wind.
Therefore, the people fervently sang of King Xuān's 宣王 virtue.
The *Shī* 詩 [Book of Odes] says:
'The states of Zhōu 周 are all joyful,
the Róng 戎 have good letters.'
It also says:
'If the country is in distress,
Zhòng Shānfǔ understood this.
Being both wise and discerning,
he preserved himself.
From morning till night, he was never lax,
in serving the one person (the king).'
Such a man could be called a savior of the world."
8.4 Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated Duke Zhuāng.
Jīng Kuǎi Ruì was on a mission to Jìn and returned.
His servant said:
"Cuī Zhù has assassinated Duke Zhuāng,
what will you do?"
Xíng Kuǎi Kuì said:
"Drive on.
I will enter and die to repay the ruler."
His servant said:
"The ruler's lack of virtue
is known to all the neighboring lords.
For you to die for him,
isn't that difficult?"
Jīng Kuǎi Ruì said:
"Well said!
If you had told me this earlier,
I could have remonstrated.
If my remonstrations were not heeded,
I could have left.
But now, having neither remonstrated,
nor left,
I have heard it said,
One who eats his food,
dies in his service.
"I have already eaten the food of a chaotic ruler,
how then could I govern this ruler and die for him?"
Thereupon, he drove his chariot and entered to die.
His servant said:
"People have a chaotic ruler,
and still must die for him.
I have a well-governed master,
how could I not die?"
Then he tied the reins and cut his own throat on the chariot.
When a *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) heard of this,
he said:
"Jīng Kuǎi Ruì can be said to have guarded his integrity and died for righteousness.
The servant, however, died without purpose,
like eating and encountering poison."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"From morning till night, never idle,
serving but one man."
This speaks of Master Jīng.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"Not constant in one's virtue,
perhaps one will bear the shame."
This speaks of the servant.
8.5 To yield and yet be straightforward
is the highest.
To remonstrate sharply
The next is remonstrance by slander.
Remonstrance by slander is the lowest.
Cowardice is equivalent to death.
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
"Softness does not mean ingestion."
8.6 Sòng Wàn fought with Duke Zhuāng.
He captured Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng was defeated and lodged in the palace.
After several months,
he was then returned to Sòng.
He returned to become a minister in Sòng.
Sòng Wàn was playing *bó* with Duke Mǐn,
and the women were all at his side.
Wàn said:
"Indeed,
the Marquis of Lǔ is virtuous,
the Marquis of Lǔ is handsome!
Among the lords of the world, the only one who should be a ruler
is the Marquis of Lǔ."
Duke Mǐn, pitying these women,
was jealous of his words,
turned his head and said:
"You are a captive,
how would you know the beauty or ugliness of the Marquis of Lǔ?"
Sòng Wàn was enraged,
and struck Duke Mǐn, severing his neck.
Chóu Mù, hearing of the assassination of his lord,
rushed to arrive,
He encountered him at the gate,
brandishing a sword and shouting at him.
Wàn Bì struck down Chóu Mù,
crushing his head,
his teeth stuck to the doorjamb.
Chóu Mù can be said to have been fearless of the powerful and oppressive.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Only Zhòng Shānfǔ,
in gentleness does not swallow,
in firmness does not vomit."
8.7 To be acceptable to the ruler,
but not to one's father,
is something a filial son would not do.
To be acceptable to one's father,
but not to the ruler,
is something a gentleman would also not do.
Therefore, the ruler cannot be usurped,
nor can one's parents be usurped.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Kind and amiable is the gentleman,
he is a model for all directions."
8.8 When the Yellow Emperor, Huángdì, ascended the throne,
he bestowed favor and received from Heaven,
single-mindedly cultivated virtue,
and only practiced benevolence.
Peace reigned within the universe.
Having not yet seen a phoenix,
he only contemplated its image.
Sleeping late and rising early,
he then summoned Tiān Lǎo 天老 and asked him,
"What is the appearance of the phoenix like?"
Tiān Lǎo 天老 replied,
"The appearance of the phoenix is such that,
it has the front of a swan and the rear of a qilin,
a snake's neck and a fish's tail,
dragon patterns and a turtle's body,
a swallow's chin and a chicken's beak.
It wears virtue and carries benevolence,
embraces loyalty and holds righteousness.
Its small sound is like metal,
its loud sound is like a drum.
It stretches its neck and vigorously flaps its wings,
with all five colors clearly displayed.
Its movements govern the eight winds,
and its breath corresponds to seasonal rain.
It eats with substance,
and drinks with decorum.
Its departure signifies the beginning of culture,
and its arrival signifies the perfection of goodness.
Only the phoenix is capable of communicating celestial blessings,
responding to earthly spirits,
harmonizing the five tones,
and discerning the nine virtues.
When the world is governed by the Dao,
if one possesses one of the phoenix's characteristics,
then the phoenix will pass by.
If one attains two aspects of the phoenix,
then the phoenix will soar (xiáng) [to that place].
If one attains three aspects of the phoenix,
then the phoenix will gather [there].
If one attains four aspects of the phoenix,
then the phoenix will descend [there] every spring and autumn.
If one attains five aspects of the phoenix,
then the phoenix will dwell [there] for life."
The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) said:
"Alas,
truly [so]!
How dare I be worthy of this!"
Thereupon, the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) put on yellow clothing,
wore a yellow crown,
and performed purification rituals in the palace.
Then the phoenix arrived, obscuring the sun.
The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) descended from the eastern steps,
faced west,
bowed twice and kowtowed, saying:
"May August Heaven (Huángtiān) bestow blessings;
I dare not disobey the mandate!"
Then the phoenix settled in the eastern region of the Emperor,
gathered on the Emperor's wutong tree,
ate the Emperor's bamboo fruit,
and dwelt [there] for life, never leaving.
The *Classic of Poetry* says:
"The phoenix flies,
its feathers soaring (huìhuì);
Yì jí yuán zhǐ."
8.9 Marquis Wèi Wén Hóu had a son named Jī,
followed by Sù.
Sù was the younger, and was established as heir.
Jī was enfeoffed in Zhōngshān,
and for three years there was no communication between them.
His tutor, Zhào Cāng Táng, said:
"A father may forget his son,
but a son must not forget his father.
Why not send an envoy?"
Jī said:
"I wish to,
but have not yet found someone to send."
Cāng Táng said:
"I request to be the envoy."
Jī said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, he inquired about what the marquis liked and what he was fond of.
He was told:
"The marquis likes northern dogs,
and is fond of morning geese."
So he sought northern dogs and morning geese to take with him.
Cāng Táng arrived,
and said:
"The lord of Zhōngshān from the northern barbarians
has northern dogs and morning geese,
and sends Cāng Táng to present them with double bows."
Wén Hóu said:
"Jī knows that I like northern dogs,
and I love morning geese."
Then he met the envoy.
Wén Hóu said:
"Is Jī well?"
Cāng Táng said "yes, yes" but did not answer.
He asked three times, but he did not answer three times.
Wén Hóu said:
"Why don't you answer?"
Cāng Táng said:
"I have heard that feudal lords do not call their rulers by their personal names.
Since you have already bestowed upon him a humble territory,
allowing him to be the lord of a small state,
if you, my lord, ask using his personal name,
I dare not answer."
Wén Hóu said:
"Is the lord of Zhōngshān well?"
Cāng Táng said:
"When I came here,
he bowed and saw me off in the suburbs."
Wén Hóu said:
"How about the lord of Zhōngshān's height?"
Cāng Táng said:
"According to propriety,
when comparing a person, one must compare them to their peers. When asking about a feudal lord,
compare him to other feudal lords.
When the feudal lords are at court,
those beside them are all subjects,
beyond compare."
"In that case, how can the bestowed garments and furs possibly surpass it?"
Wén Hóu said,
"What does the ruler of Zhōngshān like?"
He replied,
"He likes the *Shī* (Odes)."
Wén Hóu said,
"What does he like in the *Shī*?"
He said,
"He likes 'Shǔ Lí' and 'Chén Fēng'."
Wén Hóu said,
"'Shǔ Lí', what is that about?"
He replied,
"'There the millet stands thick,
